mouth.name: Mouth
mouth.definition: Chewing breaks food apart; saliva moistens it and begins starch digestion. The mouth also seeds the digestive tract with a continual flow of microbes.
summary: Chewing breaks food apart; saliva moistens it and begins starch digestion. The mouth also seeds the digestive tract with a continual flow of microbes.
Teeth, tongue, and saliva create different surfaces and oxygen gradients. Streptococci ferment sugars; Veillonella consumes lactate released by neighbouring organisms.

oesophagus.name: Oesophagus
oesophagus.definition: Coordinated muscular waves carry swallowed food into the stomach. Movement and reflux shape what reaches this habitat and how long it remains.
summary: Coordinated muscular waves carry swallowed food into the stomach. Movement and reflux shape what reaches this habitat and how long it remains.

The oesophagus carries each swallow from the mouth to the stomach. Waves of muscle move food and liquid along a moist, protective lining, while the valve at its lower end helps keep stomach contents from flowing back. Microbes arrive with saliva and food, and some live close to the surface. Swallowing, saliva and reflux shape the conditions they encounter.

stomach.name: Stomach
stomach.definition: The stomach mixes food with acid and enzymes, begins protein digestion, and meters its contents into the small intestine.
summary: The stomach mixes food with acid and enzymes, begins protein digestion, and meters its contents into the small intestine.

The stomach is a mixing chamber and a gateway between the mouth and intestine. Each meal brings a fresh supply of food and microbes into a changing landscape: acidic contents in the centre, a protective mucus layer at the wall, and pulses of nutrients as food breaks down. Many organisms pass through; others find places to persist. Acidity, meal timing, mucus and medicines shape this community.

small.name: Small intestine
small.definition: Digestion continues with bile and pancreatic enzymes. Most nutrient absorption happens here, across a vast folded surface.
summary: Digestion continues with bile and pancreatic enzymes. Most nutrient absorption happens here, across a vast folded surface.

The small intestine is where most digestion and nutrient absorption take place. Food from the stomach meets bile and digestive enzymes, then travels across a long, folded surface that takes nutrients into the body. Microbes share this changing supply of food. Their surroundings differ along the intestine as nutrients are absorbed, oxygen levels change and muscular movement carries the contents onward.

colon.name: Colon
colon.definition: Microbes ferment substrates that escape earlier digestion. The colon absorbs water and microbial products while preparing the remaining material for passage.
summary: Microbes ferment substrates that escape earlier digestion. The colon absorbs water and microbial products while preparing the remaining material for passage.

The colon receives what remains after the small intestine has absorbed most readily available nutrients. It recovers water and salts while a dense microbial community breaks down fibres and other food that has reached this far. This fermentation produces compounds used by microbes and the body. Food supply, the mucus lining and the time contents spend here shape a rich landscape of microbial partnerships.

rectum.name: Rectum
rectum.definition: The rectum stores stool before coordinated evacuation. Transit through the bowel changes microbial resources, fermentation, and the material that is eventually sampled.
summary: The rectum stores stool before coordinated evacuation. Transit through the bowel changes microbial resources, fermentation, and the material that is eventually sampled.

The rectum is the final holding area before a bowel movement. It receives stool from the colon, senses when it is filling and works with the pelvic floor and anal sphincters to control its release. The arriving stool carries microbes and products of digestion from upstream. The lining and mucus form a local habitat too, connecting this final chamber to the wider intestinal ecosystem.

streptococcus.name: Streptococcus
streptococcus.definition: Streptococcus contains many bacterial species. Many are regular inhabitants of the mouth, where they attach to teeth or soft surfaces, use sugars and help build plaque: a community held together in a sticky film.
summary: Streptococcus contains many bacterial species. Many are regular inhabitants of the mouth, where they attach to teeth or soft surfaces, use sugars and help build plaque: a community held together in a sticky film.

Fermenting sugar produces acids, including lactate. Other bacteria, such as Veillonella, use this lactate as food. Saliva, oxygen, neighbouring organisms and the frequency of sugar exposure shape what happens inside each small patch of plaque.

When plaque stays acidic repeatedly, acid-producing organisms including S. mutans contribute to mineral loss from teeth. Dental decay comes from this repeated ecological and chemical process; finding the genus Streptococcus alone does not identify decay or a need for antibiotics.

Fluoride toothpaste supports tooth mineral repair. Brushing and cleaning between teeth disrupt plaque, while reducing frequent sugary snacks gives the mouth more time away from acid production. Dental treatment addresses established decay. The goal is a functioning oral community, not the removal of all streptococci.

Swallowing also delivers streptococci to the oesophagus and stomach. Researchers have recovered them from biopsies and measured carbohydrate-processing activity in the small intestine. Those are different habitats from dental plaque, with different food supplies and conditions.

veillonella.name: Veillonella
veillonella.definition: Veillonella is a group of bacteria that often grows beside organisms making lactic acid. Instead of competing for the same sugars, it uses their lactate and releases other fermentation products, including propionate. This makes it a useful example of microbes feeding one another.
summary: Veillonella is a group of bacteria that often grows beside organisms making lactic acid. Instead of competing for the same sugars, it uses their lactate and releases other fermentation products, including propionate. This makes it a useful example of microbes feeding one another.

In the mouth it joins mixed biofilms on oral surfaces. Some oral isolates also reduce nitrate to nitrite, continuing chemistry that begins with nitrate in saliva. Swallowed nitrite then enters reactions at the acidic entrance to the stomach.

Veillonella also occurs in intestinal communities. Its growth follows the supply of lactate, the movement of contents and the activity of its bacterial neighbours. Researchers study this exchange as part of a food web rather than as an isolated population.

An athlete study found more Veillonella after marathon running. Experiments then traced blood lactate into the mouse intestine, where an isolate from a runner converted it to propionate. Giving the isolate, or propionate, increased treadmill endurance in mice. That experiment explains a route linking muscle and gut; it did not test a performance treatment in people.

For oral health, plaque control changes the whole community and its food supply. For intestinal health, research is investigating the effects of lactate exchange and bacterial products on host cells. There is no established routine treatment aimed at raising Veillonella in healthy people.

helicobacter.name: Helicobacter pylori
helicobacter.definition: Helicobacter pylori is a spiral-shaped bacterium that can make a long-term home beside the stomach lining. Many infected people feel well. In others, the infection causes persistent inflammation, called gastritis, and can lead to stomach or duodenal ulcers. Over years it also increases the risk of stomach cancer and a rare lymphoma of the stomach lining.
summary: Helicobacter pylori is a spiral-shaped bacterium that can make a long-term home beside the stomach lining. Many infected people feel well. In others, the infection causes persistent inflammation, called gastritis, and can lead to stomach or duodenal ulcers. Over years it also increases the risk of stomach cancer and a rare lymphoma of the stomach lining.

The stomach is acidic, but H. pylori builds a small refuge around itself. An acid-sensitive channel lets urea enter the cell. Its urease enzyme breaks urea down into ammonia and carbon dioxide, helping protect the bacterium from acid. Experiments in gastric mucus show that the resulting pH change also loosens the gel so the bacterium can swim through it. Its flagella propel it toward the lining.

Once established, the bacterium interacts with the stomach’s cells and immune defences. Damage depends on the strain, the person’s inflammatory response and where the infection is concentrated. This is an infection to identify and treat, rather than a population to bring toward a universal “balanced” percentage. A stool microbiome abundance score does not by itself establish active gastric infection or explain every episode of stomach discomfort.

Active infection is commonly checked with a urea breath test or a stool antigen test. Samples taken during an endoscopy can also identify it. The breath test uses the same urease chemistry: the person swallows labelled urea, and the test looks for labelled carbon dioxide in their breath.

Treatment combines acid suppression with antibiotics to clear the infection; some regimens also contain bismuth. Drug choice depends on antibiotic resistance, previous treatment and allergies. The 2024 American College of Gastroenterology guideline recommends a 14-day bismuth quadruple regimen when antibiotic susceptibility is unknown in its North American setting. Resistance patterns and available medicines shape local choices elsewhere.

Clearing H. pylori helps ulcers heal and reduces their return. A long-term randomised trial also found fewer stomach cancers after eradication. Treatment can cause side effects and temporarily change other gut microbes. Feeling better does not prove that the infection is gone: follow-up breath or stool testing confirms whether treatment worked. Antibiotics and acid-suppressing medicines affect test accuracy, so the timing of that test is planned as part of treatment.

Probiotics are being studied alongside eradication therapy, particularly for treatment side effects. They do not replace a course that clears the infection. Current research follows antibiotic resistance, the wider gastric community and the changes in the stomach lining that remain after successful treatment.

lactobacillus.name: Lactobacillus & relatives
lactobacillus.definition: Lactobacillus and its relatives are bacteria that ferment carbohydrates, commonly producing lactic acid. The old Lactobacillus genus has been divided into several genera, so familiar species now appear under names such as Limosilactobacillus. These organisms occur in foods and several human habitats.
summary: Lactobacillus and its relatives are bacteria that ferment carbohydrates, commonly producing lactic acid. The old Lactobacillus genus has been divided into several genera, so familiar species now appear under names such as Limosilactobacillus. These organisms occur in foods and several human habitats.

In the stomach, swallowed cells meet acid, food and gastric mucus. A human experiment with L. johnsonii in acidified milk studied survival through this passage. Surviving a journey and establishing a lasting population are different processes. Small-intestinal sampling shows that introduced organisms settle unevenly across people and sites.

Their products reach beyond lactate. In bacterial and human immune-cell experiments, L. reuteri 6475 converted the amino acid histidine to histamine. That histamine activated an immune-cell receptor and reduced production of the inflammatory signal TNF. The mechanism belongs to that studied organism and pathway.

Changes in diet, antibiotics and the local habitat change which members grow. A commercial probiotic trial studies a particular preparation and outcome; the name Lactobacillus on another product does not identify the same intervention. The useful question is which preparation was tested, in whom, and what changed.

Fermented foods introduce lactobacilli and their fermentation products. Experimental studies follow how long these cells survive, which metabolites they release, and how introduced strains interact with an existing community.

food_summary: The bacteria historically grouped as Lactobacillus include many specialists in fermented foods. Yoghurt commonly uses L. delbrueckii subsp. bulgaricus; vegetable ferments contain other lactic acid bacteria suited to plant sugars, salt and progressively acidic conditions.

Their production of lactic acid changes flavour, preservation and texture. Different foods select different communities: the organisms growing in milk, kefir grains and cabbage brine are connected through fermentation chemistry, while living in distinct food habitats.

bifidobacterium.name: Bifidobacterium
bifidobacterium.definition: Bifidobacterium is a group of bacteria that breaks down carbohydrates and releases acetate and lactate. Its members occupy an important place in the gut’s food-sharing network. Their populations change through infancy, adulthood and older age, alongside changes in diet and medicines.
summary: Bifidobacterium is a group of bacteria that breaks down carbohydrates and releases acetate and lactate. Its members occupy an important place in the gut’s food-sharing network. Their populations change through infancy, adulthood and older age, alongside changes in diet and medicines.

One partner’s waste becomes another partner’s fuel. In a coculture experiment, B. adolescentis supplied acetate that supported more butyrate production by F. prausnitzii. Butyrate is used by cells lining the colon. A change in one organism can therefore alter the chemistry delivered by several others.

In an E. coli infection experiment in mice, acetate-producing bifidobacteria reduced toxin passage from the gut into the blood. Separately, a human trial of B. breve A1 measured an improvement in cognitive-test scores. These experiments study different organisms, preparations and outcomes, rather than a single effect of all bifidobacteria.

Antibiotics, dietary changes and illness reshape their populations and the substrates their neighbours receive. Researchers follow both bacterial strains and acetate and lactate production to see which changes matter to the host.

Legumes, whole grains, fruit and vegetables supply different fermentable carbohydrates to this network. Some clinical trials test specific bifidobacterial preparations. The papers below identify the preparation and outcome, allowing a treatment claim to be followed back to what was actually tested.

bacteroides.name: Bacteroides
bacteroides.definition: Bacteroides is a group of bacteria with extensive machinery for taking complex carbohydrates apart. Members use different sugars from food and from mucus made by the host. Their enzymes help open food resources to a wider community of organisms.
summary: Bacteroides is a group of bacteria with extensive machinery for taking complex carbohydrates apart. Members use different sugars from food and from mucus made by the host. Their enzymes help open food resources to a wider community of organisms.

In experiments with B. thetaiotaomicron, removing dietary polysaccharides shifted bacterial activity toward the host’s mucus sugars. This illustrates how diet changes microbial behaviour as well as population size. Bacterial fermentation products also feed partners such as methane-producing archaea.

The group includes organisms with very different relationships to the host. A surface molecule from one B. fragilis strain, polysaccharide A, changed immune development in animal experiments. Other B. fragilis strains make a toxin. A genus-level stool result cannot distinguish these biological roles.

Bacteroides species can also cause infection if they reach normally protected tissues, for example after a bowel leak. That clinical problem is different from finding them in the colon, where many are ordinary community members. Antibiotic treatment of an infection is directed at the site and organism, not at eliminating the genus from a healthy gut.

A varied supply of plant carbohydrates supports different feeding opportunities. Current research follows which enzymes and metabolites are active, which strains are present and how those activities influence mucus, immunity and metabolism.

faecalibacterium.name: Faecalibacterium
faecalibacterium.definition: Faecalibacterium includes oxygen-sensitive bacteria that make butyrate during fermentation. They live within a network that shares carbohydrates and fermentation products. In coculture, F. prausnitzii uses acetate from a bifidobacterial partner and produces more butyrate.
summary: Faecalibacterium includes oxygen-sensitive bacteria that make butyrate during fermentation. They live within a network that shares carbohydrates and fermentation products. In coculture, F. prausnitzii uses acetate from a bifidobacterial partner and produces more butyrate.

Butyrate is fuel for cells lining the colon. Experiments with mouse colonocytes connected its supply to mitochondrial activity and cellular energy stores. This provides a direct route from bacterial feeding to the metabolism of the host’s own cells.

F. prausnitzii also releases molecules with effects beyond fuel supply. Researchers identified an anti-inflammatory protein called MAM that alters signalling in intestinal cells. Bacterial products and live bacteria are being investigated as different ways to reproduce useful effects.

Lower F. prausnitzii abundance has been reported in Crohn’s disease, including in studies of recurrence after surgery. Inflammation itself also changes the habitat available to oxygen-sensitive organisms. Restoring a population and treating the underlying disease are connected research questions, not interchangeable procedures.

Food fibres supply the wider fermentation network. Live Faecalibacterium treatment remains experimental: growing and delivering these oxygen-sensitive organisms is technically demanding. Work on cultured strains, defined communities and their products aims to reproduce the metabolic and anti-inflammatory effects seen in experiments.

akkermansia.name: Akkermansia muciniphila
akkermansia.definition: Akkermansia muciniphila lives close to the colon’s mucus layer and feeds on mucin, the sugar-rich material secreted by the lining. Its position brings it into contact with the host’s barrier and immune system, as well as neighbouring microbes using the products of mucin breakdown.
summary: Akkermansia muciniphila lives close to the colon’s mucus layer and feeds on mucin, the sugar-rich material secreted by the lining. Its position brings it into contact with the host’s barrier and immune system, as well as neighbouring microbes using the products of mucin breakdown.

Using mucus is part of this ecological relationship; the effect depends on how mucus production, breakdown and renewal fit together. In mice fed a high-fat diet, giving live A. muciniphila changed mucus thickness, inflammation and insulin resistance.

A small human pilot trial then tested live and pasteurised preparations. The pasteurised preparation improved insulin sensitivity and some other metabolic measures. Since the cells were no longer alive, these effects did not require a newly growing population: bacterial components can also act on the host.

The human pilot supplies a starting point for larger studies of who benefits, which preparations work and how long effects last. Researchers are also testing which bacterial components communicate with the host and how those signals change mucus renewal and metabolism.

A. muciniphila preparations are being developed as interventions. The mouse barrier experiments and human preparation trial address different pieces of that work: a living population interacting with mucus, and a measured metabolic response to a defined preparation.

methanobrevibacter.name: Methanobrevibacter
methanobrevibacter.definition: Methanobrevibacter belongs to the archaea, a separate domain of life from bacteria. These organisms use hydrogen and other fermentation products and release methane. Their growth is linked to the bacterial neighbours supplying those substrates.
summary: Methanobrevibacter belongs to the archaea, a separate domain of life from bacteria. These organisms use hydrogen and other fermentation products and release methane. Their growth is linked to the bacterial neighbours supplying those substrates.

In laboratory partnerships, M. smithii uses products released by Bacteroides. Removing hydrogen can change the conditions under which bacterial fermentation proceeds. Methane production is therefore a property of an interacting community, not an activity isolated from the rest of the gut.

Human studies link breath methane with constipation and slower bowel transit. A breath test measures gas production over time; a stool test measures material collected downstream. These measurements describe different aspects of the system and cannot be substituted directly for one another.

Constipation research brings together measured transit, medicines, diet and methane production. Following gas production over time helps investigators connect microbial activity with changes in bowel function. These observations guide clinical studies of methane-associated symptoms.

Research is expanding the archaeal family tree and testing how partnerships change fermentation and gut movement. The genome catalogue reveals further archaeal diversity beyond this familiar methane producer.

phages.name: Bacteriophages
phages.definition: Bacteriophages are viruses that infect bacteria. They do not form another bacterial genus: they depend on bacterial hosts to reproduce. Some multiply and break host cells open; others insert their genetic material into a host genome and can remain there for long periods.
summary: Bacteriophages are viruses that infect bacteria. They do not form another bacterial genus: they depend on bacterial hosts to reproduce. Some multiply and break host cells open; others insert their genetic material into a host genome and can remain there for long periods.

This creates another layer of microbial ecology. Phages change which bacterial strains survive, carry genes between organisms and respond when the bacterial habitat changes. Long-read sequencing can connect an integrated phage to its bacterial host and follow that relationship through time.

Antibiotics and faecal microbiota transplantation alter these host–virus relationships. In ulcerative colitis transplantation studies, a particular donor phage was associated with remission. That association identifies something to investigate; it does not show that the isolated phage was the treatment producing remission.

Phage therapy targets particular bacterial hosts and is being investigated for infections and microbiome interventions. Researchers select phages that can infect the relevant bacterial strain, then study how bacterial resistance and the surrounding community change the result.

The gut virome also contains viruses that infect human cells and viruses arriving with food. A large DNA-virus catalogue is one view of this diversity; it does not cover every RNA virus or every virus in one person.

fungi.name: Fungi & yeasts
fungi.definition: Fungi include yeasts and organisms that form branching filaments. Candida, Saccharomyces and Malassezia are studied in the human digestive tract. Some detected fungi arrive with food, while others can grow in the host; finding fungal DNA alone does not distinguish those situations.
summary: Fungi include yeasts and organisms that form branching filaments. Candida, Saccharomyces and Malassezia are studied in the human digestive tract. Some detected fungi arrive with food, while others can grow in the host; finding fungal DNA alone does not distinguish those situations.

Fungi interact with bacteria, mucus and immune cells. In mouse experiments, communities at the mucus surface strengthened barrier functions. Other experiments found that Malassezia restricta worsened colitis through an immune pathway involving CARD9. These organisms do not all push the system in the same direction.

Candida can grow as rounded yeast cells or as invasive filaments. Research on intestinal antibodies found that IgA preferentially targeted its more damaging filamentous form. The immune system can shape how an organism grows as well as how much of it remains.

Candida also causes recognised infections such as oral thrush and oesophageal candidiasis. Those are treated with antifungal medicines appropriate to the infected site. Simply detecting Candida in stool does not establish that it is causing intestinal symptoms or identify an antifungal treatment.

Fungal surveys, culture and experiments address different questions. The expanding research connects specific fungal species and growth forms to the host’s immune state, rather than treating all fungi as either beneficial residents or an overgrowth to remove.

prevotella.name: Prevotella
prevotella.definition: Prevotella is a diverse bacterial genus found in oral and intestinal communities. The organisms recovered from these sites are not a single population with one job.
summary: Prevotella is a diverse bacterial genus found in oral and intestinal communities. The organisms recovered from these sites are not a single population with one job.

Oral and gastric surveys place members alongside other bacteria at mucosal surfaces. Gut research follows their carbohydrate use and their response to diets. A genus label alone does not identify the species, its activity or a treatment.

rothia.name: Rothia
rothia.definition: Rothia is part of the oral community. In a human tongue study, nitrate-reducing isolates included R. mucilaginosa and R. dentocariosa.
summary: Rothia is part of the oral community. In a human tongue study, nitrate-reducing isolates included R. mucilaginosa and R. dentocariosa.
These bacteria help turn nitrate into nitrite before saliva is swallowed. The chemistry continues at the acid boundary between oesophagus and stomach.

actinomyces.name: Actinomyces
actinomyces.definition: Actinomyces includes regular members of oral communities and dental biofilms. A human tongue study recovered nitrate-reducing A. odontolyticus and A. naeslundii.
summary: Actinomyces includes regular members of oral communities and dental biofilms. A human tongue study recovered nitrate-reducing A. odontolyticus and A. naeslundii.
Those isolates connect bacterial metabolism on the tongue with swallowed nitrite. Species identification and the occupied surface provide more information than the genus name alone.

neisseria.name: Neisseria
neisseria.definition: Members of Neisseria occur among the organisms detected in the mouth and upper digestive tract. A sample from saliva, plaque or a gastric biopsy describes a different surface and environment.
summary: Members of Neisseria occur among the organisms detected in the mouth and upper digestive tract. A sample from saliva, plaque or a gastric biopsy describes a different surface and environment.

fusobacterium.name: Fusobacterium
fusobacterium.definition: Fusobacterium occurs in mixed oral communities and has also been detected in upper-digestive-tract surveys. Its species and the tissue being sampled matter for understanding what the result describes.
summary: Fusobacterium occurs in mixed oral communities and has also been detected in upper-digestive-tract surveys. Its species and the tissue being sampled matter for understanding what the result describes.

porphyromonas.name: Porphyromonas
porphyromonas.definition: Porphyromonas is one of the bacterial genera investigated in oral biofilms and gum disease. Inflamed gum pockets create a different habitat from the exposed surface of a clean tooth.
summary: Porphyromonas is one of the bacterial genera investigated in oral biofilms and gum disease. Inflamed gum pockets create a different habitat from the exposed surface of a clean tooth.
Dental care addresses the plaque community and damaged supporting tissues. A genus detected in a sample is not, by itself, a measure of how much gum disease is present.

corynebacterium.name: Corynebacterium
corynebacterium.definition: Corynebacterium forms part of the organised architecture visible in human dental plaque. Microscopy reveals bacteria arranged in structured neighbourhoods rather than an evenly mixed film.
summary: Corynebacterium forms part of the organised architecture visible in human dental plaque. Microscopy reveals bacteria arranged in structured neighbourhoods rather than an evenly mixed film.
The spatial study follows physical relationships between bacterial groups. The oral reference database connects those groups to a wider set of named and unnamed taxa.

granulicatella.name: Granulicatella
granulicatella.definition: Granulicatella appears in aerodigestive bacterial reference collections. Its presence in a sample can be followed down to a named taxon rather than being grouped under a general label such as oral flora.
summary: Granulicatella appears in aerodigestive bacterial reference collections. Its presence in a sample can be followed down to a named taxon rather than being grouped under a general label such as oral flora.

gemella.name: Gemella
gemella.definition: Gemella is represented in the oral and aerodigestive bacterial reference. It belongs to the wider community omitted by a short list of featured organisms.
summary: Gemella is represented in the oral and aerodigestive bacterial reference. It belongs to the wider community omitted by a short list of featured organisms.

haemophilus.name: Haemophilus
haemophilus.definition: Haemophilus includes members of the aerodigestive community. This genus contains several species, so a broad sequencing label should be followed to the most specific identification available.
summary: Haemophilus includes members of the aerodigestive community. This genus contains several species, so a broad sequencing label should be followed to the most specific identification available.

ruminococcus.name: Ruminococcus & related lineages
ruminococcus.definition: These names cover intestinal bacterial lineages investigated for their use of complex food carbohydrates. Modern genome taxonomies split some familiar genus names into several groups.
summary: These names cover intestinal bacterial lineages investigated for their use of complex food carbohydrates. Modern genome taxonomies split some familiar genus names into several groups.

roseburia.name: Roseburia
roseburia.definition: Roseburia includes intestinal bacteria studied for fermentation and butyrate production. It is part of a wider feeding network involving dietary substrates and products released by neighbours.
summary: Roseburia includes intestinal bacteria studied for fermentation and butyrate production. It is part of a wider feeding network involving dietary substrates and products released by neighbours.

eubacterium.name: Eubacterium & related lineages
eubacterium.definition: Eubacterium is a historical name spanning several intestinal bacterial lineages. Reclassification means that current genome catalogues and older experiments can use different names for related organisms.
summary: Eubacterium is a historical name spanning several intestinal bacterial lineages. Reclassification means that current genome catalogues and older experiments can use different names for related organisms.
Some studied members produce butyrate during fermentation.

enterobacteriaceae.name: Enterobacteriaceae
enterobacteriaceae.definition: This bacterial family includes Escherichia and several other genera. Family-level detection is a broad description: it does not identify the strain, its toxin genes or its behaviour.
summary: This bacterial family includes Escherichia and several other genera. Family-level detection is a broad description: it does not identify the strain, its toxin genes or its behaviour.

An infection experiment with toxin-producing E. coli showed that acetate from bifidobacteria reduced toxin passage across the mouse gut barrier. The host, bacterial strain and surrounding community all contributed to that outcome.

candida.name: Candida albicans
candida.definition: Candida albicans is a yeast that can also grow as branching filaments. It can be carried without symptoms, while changes in host defences allow recognised infections such as oral thrush and oesophageal candidiasis.
summary: Candida albicans is a yeast that can also grow as branching filaments. It can be carried without symptoms, while changes in host defences allow recognised infections such as oral thrush and oesophageal candidiasis.
In mouse intestinal experiments, antibodies preferentially targeted the invasive growth form. This links fungal shape to the way the immune system manages the organism.
Antifungal treatment addresses diagnosed infection and its site. A fungal DNA finding in stool does not establish that Candida is the cause of a person’s gut symptoms.

saccharomyces.name: Saccharomyces
saccharomyces.definition: Saccharomyces includes yeasts associated with food and human gut samples. Some detected cells can arrive with food, so a stool result alone does not demonstrate permanent colonisation.
summary: Saccharomyces includes yeasts associated with food and human gut samples. Some detected cells can arrive with food, so a stool result alone does not demonstrate permanent colonisation.

Fungal research follows their location, growth and interactions with intestinal immune cells. Selected preparations are also studied as probiotics; those preparations are distinct from the whole genus.

malassezia.name: Malassezia restricta
malassezia.definition: Malassezia is familiar as a skin-associated fungal genus, and M. restricta has also been studied in the intestine. Researchers connected its presence with Crohn’s disease and tested a host immune pathway in mice.
summary: Malassezia is familiar as a skin-associated fungal genus, and M. restricta has also been studied in the intestine. Researchers connected its presence with Crohn’s disease and tested a host immune pathway in mice.
In those experiments it worsened colitis through CARD9-related signalling. This is a specific fungal–immune interaction, not evidence that every fungal detection represents the same disease process.

blastocystis.name: Blastocystis
blastocystis.definition: Blastocystis is a single-celled eukaryote found in many human gut communities. It contains genetically distinct subtypes and is often detected in people without symptoms.
summary: Blastocystis is a single-celled eukaryote found in many human gut communities. It contains genetically distinct subtypes and is often detected in people without symptoms.

A study spanning 56,989 people linked its presence with healthier dietary patterns and more favourable cardiometabolic measures. That association does not establish that deliberately introducing it improves health.
Its relationship with symptoms is still being investigated. The useful distinction is between identifying the organism, identifying a subtype and demonstrating what it does in a particular host.

giardia.name: Giardia duodenalis
giardia.definition: Giardia is a flagellated single-celled parasite of the small intestine. Infection can cause diarrhoea, gas, cramps and problems absorbing nutrients. It is transmitted through swallowed cysts, including in contaminated water.
summary: Giardia is a flagellated single-celled parasite of the small intestine. Infection can cause diarrhoea, gas, cramps and problems absorbing nutrients. It is transmitted through swallowed cysts, including in contaminated water.

A stool test and clinical assessment connect the organism with a suspected infection. Antiparasitic medicines are used for symptomatic giardiasis; ongoing symptoms after treatment can also require checking for reinfection or a different cause.

cryptosporidium.name: Cryptosporidium
cryptosporidium.definition: Cryptosporidium infects the intestinal surface and can cause watery diarrhoea. Its resistant transmission stage is an oocyst, which can reach people through contaminated water or other faecal exposure.
summary: Cryptosporidium infects the intestinal surface and can cause watery diarrhoea. Its resistant transmission stage is an oocyst, which can reach people through contaminated water or other faecal exposure.
This is an infection to investigate, rather than a missing community member to restore. Illness can be more serious when immune defences are weakened.

entamoeba.name: Entamoeba histolytica
entamoeba.definition: Entamoeba histolytica is an intestinal amoeba that can invade the colon and cause dysentery. Infection can also spread beyond the intestine.
summary: Entamoeba histolytica is an intestinal amoeba that can invade the colon and cause dysentery. Infection can also spread beyond the intestine.
Several Entamoeba species look similar under basic microscopy but differ in their relationship to disease. Species identification is important when interpreting an amoeba result.

dientamoeba.name: Dientamoeba fragilis
dientamoeba.definition: Dientamoeba fragilis is a single-celled intestinal organism. It is included in clinical parasite references and can be found in people with and without gut symptoms.
summary: Dientamoeba fragilis is a single-celled intestinal organism. It is included in clinical parasite references and can be found in people with and without gut symptoms.
Finding it raises questions about symptoms, other detected organisms and the testing method. Its detection and the demonstration that it causes a particular illness are separate findings.

ascaris.name: Ascaris lumbricoides
ascaris.definition: Ascaris adults live in the small-intestinal contents, where a heavy burden can interfere with nutrition or obstruct the bowel. Infection begins with swallowing eggs that have matured in contaminated soil.
summary: Ascaris adults live in the small-intestinal contents, where a heavy burden can interfere with nutrition or obstruct the bowel. Infection begins with swallowing eggs that have matured in contaminated soil.
Before returning to the intestine as adults, larvae migrate through the body, including the lungs. The same infection therefore has an intestinal home and a wider tissue phase.
Sanitation and diagnosis-led deworming interrupt this cycle. Studies of soil-transmitted worms also examine how infection and treatment change neighbouring bacterial communities.

trichuris.name: Trichuris trichiura
trichuris.definition: The human whipworm embeds its thin front end in the lining of the caecum and ascending colon. Infection follows ingestion of mature eggs from contaminated soil or food.
summary: The human whipworm embeds its thin front end in the lining of the caecum and ascending colon. Infection follows ingestion of mature eggs from contaminated soil or food.
Light infections often produce few symptoms. Heavy burdens can cause persistent diarrhoea, abdominal pain and, especially in children, growth problems or rectal prolapse.
Stool testing identifies characteristic eggs. Research on deworming follows both parasite clearance and changes in the bacterial community that shares this habitat.

strongyloides.name: Strongyloides stercoralis
strongyloides.definition: Strongyloides stercoralis begins with larvae penetrating the skin. Adult females occupy the small-intestinal lining and produce larvae that can leave the body or start another cycle within it.
summary: Strongyloides stercoralis begins with larvae penetrating the skin. Adult females occupy the small-intestinal lining and produce larvae that can leave the body or start another cycle within it.
This internal reinfection can sustain an infection for decades. Immunosuppression, especially corticosteroids, can trigger dangerous acceleration and spread of the infection.
Diagnosis uses parasite-specific testing suited to its life cycle. Possible past exposure matters when clinicians assess someone before immunosuppressive treatment.

hookworms.name: Hookworms
hookworms.definition: Human intestinal hookworms include Necator americanus and Ancylostoma species. Adults attach to the small-intestinal lining and feed there, producing chronic blood loss when the burden is substantial.
summary: Human intestinal hookworms include Necator americanus and Ancylostoma species. Adults attach to the small-intestinal lining and feed there, producing chronic blood loss when the burden is substantial.

Infective larvae in soil commonly enter through skin, then reach the intestine after a tissue-migration phase. Iron deficiency and impaired growth connect this local intestinal infection to the rest of the body.
Diagnosis and deworming are paired with attention to anaemia and ongoing exposure. Research also studies the bacterial and immune environment shared by hookworms and their host.

crass.name: Crass-like bacteriophages
crass.definition: Crass-like phages are viruses associated with gut bacterial hosts. They sit within a large and still expanding diversity of bacterial viruses recovered from stool metagenomes.
summary: Crass-like phages are viruses associated with gut bacterial hosts. They sit within a large and still expanding diversity of bacterial viruses recovered from stool metagenomes.
The Metagenomic Gut Virus study assembled 189,680 draft viral genomes from 11,810 stool metagenomes.

temperate-phages.name: Temperate bacteriophages
temperate-phages.definition: Temperate phages can persist inside bacterial genomes. They may stay with a host lineage or enter a phase of producing new virus particles.
summary: Temperate phages can persist inside bacterial genomes. They may stay with a host lineage or enter a phase of producing new virus particles.
Long-read sequencing follows integrated viruses together with their bacterial hosts through time.

enterobius.name: Enterobius vermicularis
enterobius.definition: The human pinworm lives mainly in the caecum and adjacent colon. At night, females travel to the skin around the anus to lay eggs, often causing itching and disturbed sleep.
summary: The human pinworm lives mainly in the caecum and adjacent colon. At night, females travel to the skin around the anus to lay eggs, often causing itching and disturbed sleep.

Eggs spread through contaminated hands, bedding and surfaces. Swallowed eggs hatch in the small intestine before the worms mature in the colon. This direct cycle makes reinfection within households common.
An early-morning adhesive-tape sample can detect eggs. Clinical care combines an appropriate antiparasitic medicine with measures that interrupt household transmission.

hymenolepis.name: Hymenolepis nana
hymenolepis.definition: The dwarf tapeworm completes its adult stage in the small intestine. Unlike many tapeworms, it can pass directly between people through swallowed eggs, without requiring meat or an intermediate animal.
summary: The dwarf tapeworm completes its adult stage in the small intestine. Unlike many tapeworms, it can pass directly between people through swallowed eggs, without requiring meat or an intermediate animal.
Larvae develop in intestinal villi, then return to the lumen as adults. Internal reinfection allows an infection to persist. Heavy burdens can cause abdominal discomfort and diarrhoea.
Stool examination identifies eggs. Treatment and prevention focus on clearing infection and interrupting faecal–oral exposure.

taenia-saginata.name: Taenia saginata
taenia-saginata.definition: The beef tapeworm attaches in the small intestine after a person eats infected undercooked beef. Its segmented body releases egg-containing segments that leave with stool.
summary: The beef tapeworm attaches in the small intestine after a person eats infected undercooked beef. Its segmented body releases egg-containing segments that leave with stool.
Cattle acquire the eggs from contaminated surroundings, completing a cycle between people, cattle and food. Human infection often produces mild symptoms; seeing moving segments can be the first sign.
Laboratory identification of segments helps distinguish Taenia species. Prevention includes sanitation and adequate cooking of beef.

taenia-solium.name: Taenia solium
taenia-solium.definition: The pork tapeworm has two important human infection routes. Eating infected undercooked pork produces an adult worm in the intestine. Swallowing eggs from human faecal contamination can instead produce larval cysts in tissues, including the brain.
summary: The pork tapeworm has two important human infection routes. Eating infected undercooked pork produces an adult worm in the intestine. Swallowing eggs from human faecal contamination can instead produce larval cysts in tissues, including the brain.
These are different diseases: intestinal taeniasis and tissue cysticercosis. A person carrying an adult worm can shed eggs that expose other people.
Species identification matters because of this tissue-infection route. Diagnosis and clinical treatment depend on where the parasite is and which stage is present.

fish-tapeworm.name: Dibothriocephalus latus
fish-tapeworm.definition: The broad fish tapeworm, formerly called Diphyllobothrium latum, belongs to a group acquired from infected raw or undercooked fish. Adults attach to the small intestine using grooves on the head.
summary: The broad fish tapeworm, formerly called Diphyllobothrium latum, belongs to a group acquired from infected raw or undercooked fish. Adults attach to the small intestine using grooves on the head.

Its life cycle includes aquatic stages, small crustaceans and fish. Long adult worms produce many segments and eggs. Some infections remain unnoticed for years; others cause gastrointestinal symptoms.
Stool eggs or recovered segments support diagnosis. The CDC reference explains related fish-tapeworm species and the updated names used to distinguish them.

fasciolopsis.name: Fasciolopsis buski
fasciolopsis.definition: This large intestinal fluke is acquired by eating aquatic plants carrying encysted larvae. Snails support an earlier part of its life cycle; humans and pigs can host the adults.
summary: This large intestinal fluke is acquired by eating aquatic plants carrying encysted larvae. Snails support an earlier part of its life cycle; humans and pigs can host the adults.

After release in the duodenum, the larvae attach to the intestinal wall and mature. Light infections often cause no symptoms, while heavy infections can produce diarrhoea, abdominal pain and obstruction.
Eggs in stool support diagnosis, though their appearance overlaps with that of liver flukes. Exposure history and laboratory interpretation help identify the infection.

schistosoma.name: Schistosoma mansoni
schistosoma.definition: Schistosoma mansoni is a blood fluke with a strong intestinal connection. Adults live in veins draining the bowel, rather than freely in its contents. Eggs cross tissues toward the gut and can also become trapped in the liver.
summary: Schistosoma mansoni is a blood fluke with a strong intestinal connection. Adults live in veins draining the bowel, rather than freely in its contents. Eggs cross tissues toward the gut and can also become trapped in the liver.
Freshwater snails release larvae that penetrate human skin. Much of the tissue injury follows the immune response to eggs, linking an environmental exposure to bowel inflammation and liver disease.
Diagnosis uses the exposure history and appropriate parasite testing. The CDC reference maps the life cycle and distinguishes intestinal from urinary schistosomiasis.

trichinella.name: Trichinella spiralis
trichinella.definition: Trichinella infection begins after infected undercooked meat is eaten. Larvae released during digestion enter the small-intestinal lining and develop into short-lived adults.
summary: Trichinella infection begins after infected undercooked meat is eaten. Larvae released during digestion enter the small-intestinal lining and develop into short-lived adults.
Their offspring then migrate to skeletal muscle. This movement explains why an infection that starts with gastrointestinal symptoms can later produce muscle pain and systemic illness.
Diagnosis follows the exposure, symptoms and appropriate blood or tissue tests. The life cycle connects food preparation, the intestinal wall and tissues far beyond the gut.

leuconostoc.name: Leuconostoc
leuconostoc.definition: Leuconostoc bacteria participate in vegetable fermentations, producing organic acids and gas from plant carbohydrates. Their activity changes the environment available to the organisms that follow.
summary: Leuconostoc bacteria participate in vegetable fermentations, producing organic acids and gas from plant carbohydrates. Their activity changes the environment available to the organisms that follow.

Kimchi studies track these community changes alongside acidity and metabolites. Ingredients, storage and the microbial starting population help explain why fermentation follows different paths in different batches.

rhizopus.name: Rhizopus microsporus / oligosporus
rhizopus.definition: Food-grade Rhizopus cultures grow branching filaments through cooked soybeans. These filaments bind the beans into tempeh, while fungal enzymes change components of the substrate and develop its texture and flavour.
summary: Food-grade Rhizopus cultures grow branching filaments through cooked soybeans. These filaments bind the beans into tempeh, while fungal enzymes change components of the substrate and develop its texture and flavour.

This is a solid-state fermentation with access to oxygen. Starter experiments show that culture preparation affects performance. Tempeh is commonly cooked before eating: the meal delivers a transformed food whose nutritional value does not depend on the fungus establishing itself in the intestine.

aspergillus.name: Aspergillus oryzae
aspergillus.definition: Aspergillus oryzae is a koji mould grown on cooked grain. Its branching hyphae enter the substrate and produce enzymes that break starches and proteins into smaller molecules.
summary: Aspergillus oryzae is a koji mould grown on cooked grain. Its branching hyphae enter the substrate and produce enzymes that break starches and proteins into smaller molecules.

When koji is mixed with cooked soybeans and salt, its enzymes continue to help transform the paste. Salt-tolerant bacteria and yeasts participate in later miso maturation. The mould’s enzyme-making phase and the subsequent paste fermentation are distinct parts of the process.

zygosa.name: Zygosaccharomyces
zygosa.definition: Zygosaccharomyces includes yeasts adapted to demanding food environments. Members occur in traditional miso communities alongside bacteria and filamentous fungi.
summary: Zygosaccharomyces includes yeasts adapted to demanding food environments. Members occur in traditional miso communities alongside bacteria and filamentous fungi.

A metagenomic study comparing koji-based and spontaneous misos found differences in their dominant fungi while also detecting yeast and bacterial genera typical of miso. Those communities connect food tradition with measurable microbial ecology.

tetragenococcus.definition: Tetragenococcus bacteria occur in salty fermented-food communities, including miso. Their metabolism contributes to the changing chemistry of a paste during maturation.

The miso comparison linked here examined microbial composition across different production traditions. The food environment, its salt and its available substrates help organise which organisms grow together.

komagataeibacter.definition: These acetic-acid bacteria use oxygen to convert ethanol into organic acids. Some species weave the cellulose sheet at the surface of kombucha.
summary: These acetic-acid bacteria use oxygen to convert ethanol into organic acids. Some species weave the cellulose sheet at the surface of kombucha.

acetobacter.name: Acetobacter
acetobacter.definition: Acetobacter oxidises ethanol to acetic acid where oxygen is available. Its activity helps shape the sourness of several mixed-culture drinks.
summary: Acetobacter oxidises ethanol to acetic acid where oxygen is available. Its activity helps shape the sourness of several mixed-culture drinks.

meal-timing.name: Meal timing
meal-timing.definition: Meals create recurring changes in nutrient supply, hormone signals and intestinal activity. Fasting studies change the duration or placement of these feeding periods.
summary: Meals create recurring changes in nutrient supply, hormone signals and intestinal activity. Fasting studies change the duration or placement of these feeding periods.

streptococcus-thermophilus.name: Streptococcus thermophilus
streptococcus-thermophilus.definition: Streptococcus thermophilus is one of the two traditional yoghurt starter bacteria. In warm milk it ferments lactose and produces lactic acid. Together with Lactobacillus delbrueckii subsp. bulgaricus, it helps turn liquid milk into an acidic protein gel.
summary: Streptococcus thermophilus is one of the two traditional yoghurt starter bacteria. In warm milk it ferments lactose and produces lactic acid. Together with Lactobacillus delbrueckii subsp. bulgaricus, it helps turn liquid milk into an acidic protein gel.

The partnership changes the nutrients available to each bacterium during culturing. Cooling slows their activity. When live-culture yoghurt is eaten, microbial enzymes can also participate in lactose digestion.

saccharomyces-cerevisiae.name: Saccharomyces cerevisiae
saccharomyces-cerevisiae.definition: Saccharomyces yeasts use sugars and can produce carbon dioxide and ethanol during fermentation. In bread starters they live alongside acid-producing bacteria; in kefir they participate in a different community carried by the grains.
summary: Saccharomyces yeasts use sugars and can produce carbon dioxide and ethanol during fermentation. In bread starters they live alongside acid-producing bacteria; in kefir they participate in a different community carried by the grains.

Studies of sourdough connect yeast–bacterial interactions with aroma and dough rise. Baking kills most starter organisms, leaving their transformations in the loaf. Live fermented drinks and baked foods therefore deliver different microbial products and living populations.

condition:ibs.name: Irritable bowel syndrome
condition:ibs.definition: IBS combines recurrent abdominal pain with changes in stool frequency or consistency.
summary: IBS combines recurrent abdominal pain with changes in stool frequency or consistency. Constipation, diarrhoea and mixed patterns describe different experiences of the disorder.
Fermentation, intestinal transit, visceral sensitivity and gut–brain signalling interact. Research examines how microbial metabolites affect these processes and how dietary changes alter symptoms.
Assessment looks at the symptom pattern and features suggesting another condition. Treatment can combine dietary adjustments, soluble fibre, medicines and gut-directed psychological therapies.

condition:constipation.name: Chronic constipation
condition:constipation.definition: Constipation involves difficult, infrequent or incomplete bowel movements.
summary: Constipation involves difficult, infrequent or incomplete bowel movements. Stool hardness, straining and a sense of blockage can matter as much as how often someone goes.
Time spent in the colon changes water absorption and microbial metabolism. Methane-producing archaea are studied in relation to slower transit, alongside pelvic-floor and medication effects.
Care starts with the pattern, medicines and examination. Fibre, fluid, activity, laxatives or pelvic-floor treatment address different causes; bleeding or persistent new symptoms deserve assessment.

condition:microscopic-colitis.name: Microscopic colitis
condition:microscopic-colitis.definition: Microscopic colitis causes chronic watery diarrhoea, often without visible bleeding.
summary: Microscopic colitis causes chronic watery diarrhoea, often without visible bleeding. The colon can look normal during endoscopy; tissue samples reveal the inflammation.
Researchers study the intestinal barrier, bile acids, medication exposure and microbial communities in the inflamed colon. These are distinct targets from the visible lesions of ulcerative colitis.
Diagnosis requires colonic biopsies. Care includes reviewing medicines and triggers, managing fluid loss and using treatments such as budesonide when indicated.

condition:crohns.name: Crohn’s disease
condition:crohns.definition: Crohn’s disease produces patchy inflammation anywhere along the digestive tract.
summary: Crohn’s disease produces patchy inflammation anywhere along the digestive tract. It can affect the full bowel wall and cause pain, diarrhoea, weight loss, narrowing or fistulas.

The immune system interacts abnormally with intestinal contents and microbes. Human studies identify changes in community function; experiments investigate barrier damage, microbial products and inflammatory responses.
Endoscopy, imaging, laboratory tests and biopsies help establish the diagnosis. Anti-inflammatory or immune-targeted medicines, nutritional support and sometimes surgery control complications.

condition:ulcerative-colitis.name: Ulcerative colitis
condition:ulcerative-colitis.definition: Ulcerative colitis inflames the colon’s inner lining, usually beginning in the rectum.
summary: Ulcerative colitis inflames the colon’s inner lining, usually beginning in the rectum. Bloody diarrhoea, urgency and abdominal pain can alternate with periods of remission.
Microbial metabolites, mucus and mucosal immune responses are active research areas. Donor-microbiota trials investigate whether changing a community can help induce remission.
Treatment depends on extent and severity and can include mesalamine, immune-targeted therapy or surgery. Follow-up also addresses nutrition and colorectal-cancer surveillance.

condition:coeliac.name: Coeliac disease
condition:coeliac.definition: Coeliac disease is an immune response to gluten that damages the small-intestinal lining.
summary: Coeliac disease is an immune response to gluten that damages the small-intestinal lining. It can cause diarrhoea, bloating, iron deficiency or symptoms beyond digestion.
Damaged villi change nutrient absorption and the substrates available to microbes. Studies examine microbial gluten processing and the community’s interaction with intestinal immunity.
Blood tests and sometimes intestinal biopsy support diagnosis while gluten is still being eaten. Treatment is a lifelong gluten-free diet with attention to nutritional recovery.

condition:gerd.name: Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease
condition:gerd.definition: GERD occurs when reflux repeatedly causes troublesome symptoms or tissue injury.
summary: GERD occurs when reflux repeatedly causes troublesome symptoms or tissue injury. Heartburn and regurgitation are common; some people develop inflammation or narrowing of the oesophagus.

The oesophagus and stomach contain distinct microbial habitats. Research examines reflux-associated changes in these communities and the effects of acid-suppressing medicines on downstream gut ecology.
Care can include adjusting meal timing, addressing individual triggers and acid suppression. Swallowing difficulty, bleeding or unexplained weight loss call for assessment.

condition:functional-dyspepsia.name: Functional dyspepsia
condition:functional-dyspepsia.definition: Functional dyspepsia causes persistent upper-abdominal discomfort, early fullness or burning without a structural explanation for the symptoms.
summary: Functional dyspepsia causes persistent upper-abdominal discomfort, early fullness or burning without a structural explanation for the symptoms. It can overlap with IBS.
Research follows stomach accommodation, gastric emptying, duodenal immune activity and microbial exposure. H. pylori infection is a separate, testable contributor to dyspeptic symptoms.
Evaluation considers H. pylori, medicines and warning signs. Treatment is tailored to pain, fullness and the person’s other findings.

condition:peptic-ulcer.name: Peptic ulcer disease
condition:peptic-ulcer.definition: Peptic ulcers are breaks in the lining of the stomach or duodenum.
summary: Peptic ulcers are breaks in the lining of the stomach or duodenum. H. pylori infection and anti-inflammatory pain medicines are major causes; ulcers can bleed or perforate.
H. pylori is a direct microbial cause, working within the stomach’s mucus and acid environment. Ulcers caused by medicines follow another route to injury.
Testing and treatment address H. pylori, acid exposure and ulcer-provoking medicines. Vomiting blood, black stools or sudden severe abdominal pain need urgent care.

condition:gastritis.name: Gastritis
condition:gastritis.definition: Gastritis is inflammation of the stomach lining.
summary: Gastritis is inflammation of the stomach lining. H. pylori, autoimmune disease and other exposures can produce different forms, with or without obvious symptoms.
The gastric environment selects acid-tolerant organisms. H. pylori-driven inflammation and autoimmune loss of acid-producing cells change that environment in different ways.
Investigation may include H. pylori testing, blood tests or endoscopy. Treatment follows the cause and can also address iron or vitamin B12 deficiency.

condition:lactose-intolerance.name: Lactose intolerance
condition:lactose-intolerance.definition: Lactose intolerance causes gas, bloating or diarrhoea when too little lactase is available to digest milk sugar.
summary: Lactose intolerance causes gas, bloating or diarrhoea when too little lactase is available to digest milk sugar. The amount tolerated varies with the food and portion.
Undigested lactose reaches microbes that ferment it into acids and gases. Live yoghurt cultures can supply enzymes that assist lactose digestion during a meal.
People often manage symptoms by adjusting portions, choosing low-lactose foods or using lactase. New symptoms after an infection or bowel disease can reflect temporary loss of lactase.

condition:fructose-malabsorption.name: Fructose malabsorption
condition:fructose-malabsorption.definition: Poor absorption of a large fructose load can leave sugar in the intestine, producing bloating, gas and loose stools.
summary: Poor absorption of a large fructose load can leave sugar in the intestine, producing bloating, gas and loose stools. This differs from hereditary fructose intolerance.
Unabsorbed fructose draws water and becomes a fermentation substrate. Its effects depend on dose, accompanying sugars, transit and the microbial community.
A dietary history helps identify the pattern. A dietitian can guide targeted changes and reintroduction without unnecessarily excluding broad groups of fruit or vegetables.

condition:sibo.name: Small-intestinal bacterial overgrowth
condition:sibo.definition: SIBO describes excessive or altered bacterial growth in the small intestine.
summary: SIBO describes excessive or altered bacterial growth in the small intestine. It can accompany impaired motility, altered anatomy or other disease and produce bloating, diarrhoea or malabsorption.
Location matters: organisms and fermentation processes that belong further downstream encounter nutrients earlier. Breath gases provide an indirect measurement of this activity.
Assessment considers the underlying cause and the limitations of breath testing. Treatment may involve antibiotics, correcting contributing conditions and nutritional support.

condition:gallstones.name: Gallstones
condition:gallstones.definition: Gallstones form from components of bile.
summary: Gallstones form from components of bile. Many cause no symptoms; a stone blocking a duct can cause severe pain, infection or pancreatitis.
The liver–bile–gut circuit connects digestion with microbial bile-acid transformations. Studies examine how these transformations and metabolic conditions relate to stone formation.
Symptomatic stones often require gallbladder removal or procedures to clear a duct. Fever, jaundice or persistent severe upper-abdominal pain require prompt assessment.

condition:acute-pancreatitis.name: Acute pancreatitis
condition:acute-pancreatitis.definition: Acute pancreatitis is sudden inflammation of the pancreas.
summary: Acute pancreatitis is sudden inflammation of the pancreas. Gallstones and alcohol are common causes, and severe disease can affect circulation and other organs.
Severe inflammation can disturb gut motility and barrier function. Research studies microbial translocation and nutrition during recovery, alongside the pancreatic injury itself.
Hospital care addresses fluids, pain, nutrition and the cause. Severe persistent upper-abdominal pain with vomiting needs urgent medical attention.

condition:chronic-pancreatitis.name: Chronic pancreatitis
condition:chronic-pancreatitis.definition: Repeated or persistent pancreatic injury can cause scarring, chronic pain and loss of digestive enzyme production.
summary: Repeated or persistent pancreatic injury can cause scarring, chronic pain and loss of digestive enzyme production. Diabetes and poor nutrient absorption can follow.
Changes in enzyme delivery alter what is digested before reaching intestinal microbes. Malabsorption and microbial overgrowth can compound nutritional problems.
Care addresses the cause, pain, nutrition and diabetes. Pancreatic enzyme replacement supports digestion when enzyme production is insufficient.

condition:fatty-liver.name: Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease
condition:fatty-liver.definition: MASLD involves excess liver fat in a metabolic setting such as insulin resistance or obesity.
summary: MASLD involves excess liver fat in a metabolic setting such as insulin resistance or obesity. Some people develop inflammation, fibrosis and eventually cirrhosis.
Blood from the intestine flows directly to the liver. Microbial products, bile acids and intestinal permeability are investigated along this gut–liver route.
Assessment estimates liver injury and fibrosis as well as metabolic risk. Nutrition, sustained activity, weight management and appropriate medical treatment support liver health.

condition:diverticular-disease.name: Diverticular disease
condition:diverticular-disease.definition: Diverticula are pouches in the colon wall.
summary: Diverticula are pouches in the colon wall. They are common with age; some people develop associated pain, bleeding or inflammation.
Stool consistency, transit and diet shape the environment around the pouches. Microbial and immune changes are investigated in symptomatic disease.
Care depends on whether the issue is symptoms, bleeding or acute inflammation. Gradual dietary fibre changes can support bowel function after assessment.

condition:diverticulitis.name: Diverticulitis
condition:diverticulitis.definition: Diverticulitis occurs when one or more colonic pouches become inflamed.
summary: Diverticulitis occurs when one or more colonic pouches become inflamed. It can cause localised pain and fever, with abscesses or perforation in complicated cases.
The local bowel wall and its microbes are involved in inflammation. This differs from simply having diverticula or a particular stool-community profile.
Clinical assessment and sometimes imaging establish severity. Treatment ranges from supportive care to antibiotics, drainage or surgery for specific complications.

condition:appendicitis.name: Appendicitis
condition:appendicitis.definition: Appendicitis is inflammation of the appendix.
summary: Appendicitis is inflammation of the appendix. Pain often progresses and localises to the lower-right abdomen, sometimes with nausea or fever.
The appendix contains lymphoid tissue and a dense microbial community. Research examines obstruction, local bacterial growth and immune responses during inflammation.
Suspected appendicitis needs urgent assessment. Surgery and, in selected cases, antibiotics are treatment options chosen according to severity and complications.

condition:haemorrhoids.name: Haemorrhoids
condition:haemorrhoids.definition: Haemorrhoids are enlarged vascular cushions around the anus and lower rectum.
summary: Haemorrhoids are enlarged vascular cushions around the anus and lower rectum. They can cause bleeding, itching, discomfort or prolapse.
The practical gut connection is stool consistency and straining. Supporting comfortable bowel movements reduces repeated mechanical stress.
Care often starts with fibre, fluid and bowel habits, with procedures for persistent problems. Rectal bleeding should be assessed rather than automatically attributed to haemorrhoids.

condition:anal-fissure.name: Anal fissure
condition:anal-fissure.definition: An anal fissure is a tear in the anal lining, often causing sharp pain during bowel movements and a small amount of bright blood..
summary: An anal fissure is a tear in the anal lining, often causing sharp pain during bowel movements and a small amount of bright blood.
Hard stool, diarrhoea and sphincter tension can perpetuate injury. The relevant ecological route is through transit and stool properties rather than a named pathogenic organism.
Softening stool and treating pain support healing. Persistent fissures may need prescribed topical treatment or a procedure after examination.

condition:gastroparesis.name: Gastroparesis
condition:gastroparesis.definition: Gastroparesis slows stomach emptying without a physical blockage.
summary: Gastroparesis slows stomach emptying without a physical blockage. Early fullness, nausea, vomiting and difficulty maintaining nutrition can result.
Delayed delivery of food changes conditions along the digestive tract. Gastric motility, diabetes-related nerve changes and downstream bacterial overgrowth are related research areas.
Diagnosis usually involves an emptying study after excluding obstruction. Meals, medicines, glucose management and nutritional support are adjusted to the severity.

condition:pancreatic-insufficiency.name: Exocrine pancreatic insufficiency
condition:pancreatic-insufficiency.definition: Exocrine pancreatic insufficiency means too few pancreatic enzymes reach the intestine.
summary: Exocrine pancreatic insufficiency means too few pancreatic enzymes reach the intestine. Fatty stools, weight loss and deficiencies of fat-soluble vitamins can result.
Poorly digested nutrients change microbial substrate supply. The primary problem is enzyme delivery, which can coexist with changes in the intestinal community.
Evaluation can include stool elastase and assessment of the underlying pancreatic disease. Enzyme replacement with meals and nutritional monitoring are central to care.

condition:colorectal-cancer.name: Colorectal cancer
condition:colorectal-cancer.definition: Colorectal cancer begins in the colon or rectum, often developing through precancerous growths.
summary: Colorectal cancer begins in the colon or rectum, often developing through precancerous growths. Screening can identify lesions before symptoms appear.
Studies investigate microbial toxins, inflammation and organisms such as Fusobacterium nucleatum in tumours. Diet, metabolites and the local tissue environment are part of this research.
Screening, colonoscopy and tissue diagnosis guide care. Treatment depends on location, stage and tumour biology and can include surgery and systemic therapies.

condition:stomach-cancer.name: Stomach cancer
condition:stomach-cancer.definition: Stomach cancer can develop after long-standing changes in the gastric lining.
summary: Stomach cancer can develop after long-standing changes in the gastric lining. H. pylori is an important cause of non-cardia gastric cancer.
This is a major example of a microbial infection contributing to cancer risk. Long-term trials follow how eradicating H. pylori changes that risk.
Endoscopy and biopsy establish the diagnosis. Treatment depends on stage and tumour features; treating H. pylori is also important in prevention and relevant follow-up.

condition:salmonellosis.name: Salmonellosis
condition:salmonellosis.definition: Non-typhoidal Salmonella commonly causes diarrhoea, fever and abdominal cramps after contaminated food or contact.
summary: Non-typhoidal Salmonella commonly causes diarrhoea, fever and abdominal cramps after contaminated food or contact. Severe infection can enter the bloodstream.
Salmonella interacts with intestinal microbes and uses the inflamed gut environment to compete. Colonisation resistance and host inflammation are studied together.
Replacing lost fluids is central. Antibiotics are reserved for particular patients or severe infection; dehydration, blood in stool or persistent fever require assessment.

condition:campylobacteriosis.name: Campylobacter infection
condition:campylobacteriosis.definition: Campylobacter infection is a common foodborne cause of diarrhoea and abdominal pain.
summary: Campylobacter infection is a common foodborne cause of diarrhoea and abdominal pain. Undercooked poultry, contaminated water and animal contact are common routes.
The bacterium infects the intestinal lining and can trigger inflammation. Some people develop post-infectious IBS or other complications after the acute infection resolves.
Most cases improve with supportive care. Severe illness or higher-risk patients may need antibiotics selected with local resistance in mind.

condition:shigellosis.name: Shigellosis
condition:shigellosis.definition: Shigella spreads readily by the faecal–oral route and can cause fever, cramps and bloody diarrhoea.
summary: Shigella spreads readily by the faecal–oral route and can cause fever, cramps and bloody diarrhoea. Small inocula can cause infection.
The organism invades the colonic lining and provokes inflammation. Microbial competition, mucosal immunity and antimicrobial resistance shape infection research.
Fluid replacement and infection control matter. Testing can help guide antibiotic treatment because resistance patterns vary and increasingly limit options.

condition:stec.name: Shiga toxin-producing E. coli infection
condition:stec.definition: STEC infection can cause severe abdominal cramps and bloody diarrhoea.
summary: STEC infection can cause severe abdominal cramps and bloody diarrhoea. Shiga toxin can damage blood vessels and cause haemolytic uraemic syndrome.
This is a strain-specific pathogenic function within a much larger E. coli group. Toxin production and host susceptibility explain why species names alone are insufficient.
Suspected infection needs clinical assessment and stool testing. Antibiotics and anti-diarrhoeal medicines can be inappropriate in STEC; hydration and monitoring for complications are important.

condition:rotavirus.name: Rotavirus gastroenteritis
condition:rotavirus.definition: Rotavirus causes vomiting and diarrhoea, particularly in young children, and can produce dangerous dehydration.
summary: Rotavirus causes vomiting and diarrhoea, particularly in young children, and can produce dangerous dehydration. Vaccination has greatly reduced severe disease.
The virus infects intestinal cells. Research examines how intestinal communities and immune development influence infection and oral-vaccine responses.
Oral rehydration is central, with urgent care for significant dehydration. Vaccination is an effective preventive measure according to the local childhood schedule.

condition:cryptosporidiosis.name: Cryptosporidiosis
condition:cryptosporidiosis.definition: Cryptosporidium is a protozoal parasite that causes watery diarrhoea, often after contaminated water or contact.
summary: Cryptosporidium is a protozoal parasite that causes watery diarrhoea, often after contaminated water or contact. Disease can be persistent in people with weakened immunity.
The parasite develops at the intestinal cell surface. Nutritional status, immunity and interactions with the surrounding microbial community affect the research questions.
Treatment addresses dehydration, the parasite when indicated and immune status. Persistent or severe diarrhoea warrants assessment; water and hygiene measures reduce transmission.

condition:amoebiasis.name: Amoebiasis
condition:amoebiasis.definition: Entamoeba histolytica can cause colitis and bloody diarrhoea and sometimes spreads to the liver.
summary: Entamoeba histolytica can cause colitis and bloody diarrhoea and sometimes spreads to the liver. Other Entamoeba species have different clinical significance.
The parasite interacts with mucus, bacteria and host tissue. Distinguishing pathogenic E. histolytica from other species matters more than finding the genus name alone.
Diagnosis uses appropriate stool or other tests. Treatment targets invasive infection and organisms remaining in the bowel, with regimens chosen by a clinician.

condition:ascariasis.name: Ascariasis
condition:ascariasis.definition: Ascaris roundworms are acquired by swallowing eggs from contaminated soil or food.
summary: Ascaris roundworms are acquired by swallowing eggs from contaminated soil or food. Heavy infections can impair nutrition or obstruct the bowel.
The worms inhabit the intestinal environment and interact with host immune responses. Their life cycle also includes migration through tissues before intestinal maturation.
Diagnosis and deworming address established infection. Sanitation and preventing soil contamination interrupt transmission; severe abdominal symptoms need assessment.

condition:hookworm.name: Hookworm infection
condition:hookworm.definition: Hookworm larvae usually enter through contaminated soil and develop into worms attached to the intestine.
summary: Hookworm larvae usually enter through contaminated soil and develop into worms attached to the intestine. Chronic blood loss can cause iron-deficiency anaemia.
The worms feed at the lining and alter local immune activity. Iron status, nutrition and intestinal infection are directly connected in the disease process.
Anthelmintic treatment and correction of iron deficiency address different parts of recovery. Footwear and sanitation reduce exposure in endemic settings.

condition:trichuriasis.name: Whipworm infection
condition:trichuriasis.definition: Trichuris whipworms infect the large intestine after eggs are swallowed.
summary: Trichuris whipworms infect the large intestine after eggs are swallowed. Heavy burdens can cause abdominal pain, diarrhoea, anaemia and impaired growth.
Attachment in the bowel lining creates a sustained host–parasite interaction. Worm burden and nutrition matter alongside any accompanying bacterial-community changes.
Deworming and nutritional recovery are central. Safe sanitation and reducing soil contamination prevent repeated exposure.

condition:strongyloidiasis.name: Strongyloidiasis
condition:strongyloidiasis.definition: Strongyloides can maintain infection through an internal reinfection cycle for years.
summary: Strongyloides can maintain infection through an internal reinfection cycle for years. It may produce abdominal or skin symptoms and becomes dangerous during immunosuppression.
Its life cycle crosses the intestine and other tissues. Autoinfection distinguishes it from many other intestinal worms and explains persistent infection.
