Exposure history and appropriate testing matter before immunosuppression in at-risk people. Ivermectin-based treatment is prescribed for confirmed or clinically relevant infection.

condition:pinworm.name: Pinworm infection
condition:pinworm.definition: Pinworms commonly affect children and households, causing night-time itching around the anus.
summary: Pinworms commonly affect children and households, causing night-time itching around the anus. Eggs spread through hands and contaminated surfaces.
The parasite’s reproductive cycle involves the large intestine and perianal skin. Symptoms arise from that cycle rather than a general loss of bacterial diversity.
Treatment often addresses household transmission as well as the infected person. Handwashing, short nails and washing bedding help reduce reinfection.

condition:hepatitis-a.name: Hepatitis A
condition:hepatitis-a.definition: Hepatitis A is a liver infection spread through contaminated food, water or close contact.
summary: Hepatitis A is a liver infection spread through contaminated food, water or close contact. It can cause fatigue, nausea and jaundice.
The transmission route is enteric, while the main tissue injury is in the liver. This separates the route of exposure from the organ affected.
Supportive care and monitoring address illness. Vaccination and post-exposure measures prevent infection in relevant settings; severe vomiting or worsening jaundice needs assessment.

condition:hepatitis-b.name: Hepatitis B
condition:hepatitis-b.definition: Hepatitis B spreads through infected blood and body fluids and can become chronic.
summary: Hepatitis B spreads through infected blood and body fluids and can become chronic. Persistent infection increases the risk of cirrhosis and liver cancer.
The gut–liver circulation becomes relevant as liver disease changes bile handling and intestinal physiology. The causative agent itself is a hepatitis virus, not a gut bacterium.
Blood tests establish infection and assess activity. Vaccination prevents infection; monitoring and antiviral therapy address chronic disease when indicated.

condition:hepatitis-c.name: Hepatitis C
condition:hepatitis-c.definition: Hepatitis C is a blood-borne viral infection that often becomes chronic and can scar the liver.
summary: Hepatitis C is a blood-borne viral infection that often becomes chronic and can scar the liver. Symptoms can be absent for many years.
Liver injury changes the host environment of the gut–liver axis. Researchers follow intestinal permeability and metabolites alongside viral clearance and liver recovery.
Screening and confirmatory RNA testing identify infection. Direct-acting antiviral medicines cure most treated infections, with follow-up tailored to liver damage and other risks.

condition:cholera.name: Cholera
condition:cholera.definition: Cholera is an intestinal infection that can cause rapid, profuse watery diarrhoea.
summary: Cholera is an intestinal infection that can cause rapid, profuse watery diarrhoea. Severe fluid loss can become life-threatening within hours.
Toxigenic Vibrio cholerae alters intestinal fluid secretion. The disease illustrates a specific microbial mechanism producing a large physiological effect.
Prompt oral or intravenous rehydration saves lives. Antibiotics are used in selected cases; safe water, sanitation and vaccination help prevent outbreaks.

condition:typhoid.name: Typhoid fever
condition:typhoid.definition: Typhoid is a systemic infection caused by Salmonella Typhi, usually acquired through contaminated food or water.
summary: Typhoid is a systemic infection caused by Salmonella Typhi, usually acquired through contaminated food or water. Prolonged fever and abdominal symptoms are common.
The organism enters through the intestine and can spread through the body. Persistent carriage and antimicrobial resistance are important parts of its ecology.
Diagnosis and effective antibiotics are essential. The regimen depends on local resistance and travel history; vaccination and safe water reduce risk.

condition:oral-thrush.name: Oral thrush
condition:oral-thrush.definition: Oral thrush is overgrowth of Candida in the mouth, producing white patches or soreness.
summary: Oral thrush is overgrowth of Candida in the mouth, producing white patches or soreness. Antibiotics, dentures and immune or metabolic conditions can contribute.
A normally resident yeast expands in a changed local environment. The mouth is its own habitat; oral overgrowth does not establish that there is invasive intestinal candidiasis.
Care addresses the local infection and contributing factors, with antifungal treatment when needed. Recurrent episodes can prompt assessment of medicines or underlying conditions.

condition:vaginal-candidiasis.name: Vulvovaginal candidiasis
condition:vaginal-candidiasis.definition: Vulvovaginal candidiasis causes itching, irritation and discharge when Candida produces symptomatic infection.
summary: Vulvovaginal candidiasis causes itching, irritation and discharge when Candida produces symptomatic infection. It can recur, and other conditions can cause similar symptoms.
The vaginal ecosystem has different chemistry and community structure from the gut. Research examines fungal growth, local immunity and exchanges between neighbouring body sites.
Diagnosis helps distinguish yeast infection from other causes. Antifungal treatment and, for recurrent disease, a tailored assessment guide care.

condition:bacterial-vaginosis.name: Bacterial vaginosis
condition:bacterial-vaginosis.definition: Bacterial vaginosis involves a shift in the vaginal microbial community and can cause a characteristic discharge or odour.
summary: Bacterial vaginosis involves a shift in the vaginal microbial community and can cause a characteristic discharge or odour. Recurrence is common.

This is a site-specific community change, often involving reduced lactobacillus dominance and expansion of anaerobes. It offers a clear example of habitat chemistry and community structure interacting.
Clinical assessment or testing establishes the diagnosis. Antibiotic treatment and management of recurrence follow clinical guidance.

condition:uti.name: Urinary tract infection
condition:uti.definition: UTIs occur when microbes establish infection in the urinary tract.
summary: UTIs occur when microbes establish infection in the urinary tract. Burning, urgency and frequency are common in bladder infection; fever or flank pain can signal kidney involvement.
Gut-associated bacteria, especially particular E. coli strains, can serve as a reservoir for urinary infection. The route between habitats is central to recurrence research.
Symptoms, urine testing and sometimes culture guide treatment. Fever, flank pain, pregnancy or systemic illness change the urgency and choice of care.

condition:kidney-stones.name: Kidney stones
condition:kidney-stones.definition: Kidney stones form when substances crystallise in urine.
summary: Kidney stones form when substances crystallise in urine. They can cause severe flank pain, blood in urine or obstruction.
Some intestinal organisms metabolise oxalate, and bowel disease or altered absorption can increase urinary stone risk. This is one route linking intestinal chemistry to another organ.
Treatment depends on stone size, location and infection. Prevention uses stone analysis, urine measurements, fluid intake and targeted dietary or medical changes.

condition:ckd.name: Chronic kidney disease
condition:ckd.definition: CKD is a persistent reduction in kidney function or evidence of kidney damage.
summary: CKD is a persistent reduction in kidney function or evidence of kidney damage. Diabetes and high blood pressure are common causes.
Microbial products normally cleared by the kidneys can accumulate as function declines. Urea reaching the intestine also changes the microbial environment, creating a two-way gut–kidney interaction.
Blood and urine tests track kidney function and albumin loss. Treatment addresses the cause, blood pressure, metabolic risks and complications, with individual dietary advice.

condition:type-2-diabetes.name: Type 2 diabetes
condition:type-2-diabetes.definition: Type 2 diabetes combines insulin resistance with inadequate insulin production, leading to high blood glucose.
summary: Type 2 diabetes combines insulin resistance with inadequate insulin production, leading to high blood glucose. It affects blood vessels, nerves and other organs over time.

Studies investigate microbial metabolites, bile acids and immune signalling in glucose regulation. Medicines such as metformin also change gut communities, so treatment and disease effects need to be examined together.
Glucose monitoring, nutrition, movement and medicines support control. Care also addresses cardiovascular and kidney risks rather than glucose alone.

condition:type-1-diabetes.name: Type 1 diabetes
condition:type-1-diabetes.definition: Type 1 diabetes results from immune destruction of insulin-producing cells.
summary: Type 1 diabetes results from immune destruction of insulin-producing cells. Insulin replacement is essential, and onset can include thirst, frequent urination and weight loss.

Longitudinal studies investigate the intestinal community and immune development before diagnosis. Microbial changes are studied as part of disease development, distinct from the need for insulin treatment.
Insulin, glucose monitoring, education and nutrition are central. Vomiting, dehydration or rapid breathing with high glucose can indicate an emergency.

condition:obesity.name: Obesity
condition:obesity.definition: Obesity involves excess adiposity that can affect metabolic, mechanical and psychological health.
summary: Obesity involves excess adiposity that can affect metabolic, mechanical and psychological health. Genetics, food environments, sleep, medicines and physiology all contribute.

Microbes participate in energy extraction, metabolite production and host signalling. Studies of microbial interventions sit alongside research on diet, appetite regulation and the host’s metabolic state.
Care is individualised and can include nutritional support, activity, behavioural approaches, medicines or surgery. Health outcomes and sustained function matter alongside body weight.

condition:metabolic-syndrome.name: Metabolic syndrome
condition:metabolic-syndrome.definition: Metabolic syndrome groups abdominal adiposity, raised blood pressure, abnormal blood lipids and impaired glucose regulation.
summary: Metabolic syndrome groups abdominal adiposity, raised blood pressure, abnormal blood lipids and impaired glucose regulation. Together these increase cardiovascular and diabetes risk.
Dietary substrates, microbial metabolites and liver–gut signalling are investigated across these connected features.
Care addresses blood pressure, glucose, lipids, food patterns and activity together. Treatment can include medicines targeted to the individual risks.

condition:hypertension.name: High blood pressure
condition:hypertension.definition: Hypertension is persistently raised blood pressure, often without symptoms.
summary: Hypertension is persistently raised blood pressure, often without symptoms. Over time it damages the heart, brain, blood vessels and kidneys.
Research follows short-chain fatty acids, immune signalling and kidney–gut interactions. Dietary patterns can change both microbial substrates and blood pressure through several routes.
Repeated measurements establish the pattern. Activity, dietary changes and appropriate medicines reduce risk; management is based on measured pressure and overall health.

condition:coronary-heart-disease.name: Coronary heart disease
condition:coronary-heart-disease.definition: Coronary disease develops when atherosclerosis limits blood flow to the heart.
summary: Coronary disease develops when atherosclerosis limits blood flow to the heart. It can cause angina or an acute heart attack.

Microbial metabolism of dietary compounds, including the trimethylamine pathway, is investigated in vascular disease. These studies connect food, liver processing, kidney clearance and cardiovascular risk.
Care addresses lipids, blood pressure, smoking and other risks, with medicines and procedures when needed. New chest pressure or symptoms suggesting a heart attack require emergency care.

condition:heart-failure.name: Heart failure
condition:heart-failure.definition: Heart failure means the heart cannot fill or pump adequately for the body’s needs.
summary: Heart failure means the heart cannot fill or pump adequately for the body’s needs. Breathlessness, fatigue and swelling are common.
Reduced blood flow and congestion can change intestinal function. Microbial metabolites and barrier changes are studied along this gut–heart route.
Assessment identifies the heart problem and contributing conditions. Medicines, monitoring and sometimes devices or procedures improve symptoms and outcomes.

condition:stroke.name: Stroke
condition:stroke.definition: A stroke occurs when brain blood flow is blocked or a blood vessel ruptures.
summary: A stroke occurs when brain blood flow is blocked or a blood vessel ruptures. Sudden weakness, speech problems or visual changes are warning signs.
The gut–brain axis is investigated during inflammation and recovery after stroke. Feeding, mobility and medications also reshape the intestinal environment during rehabilitation.
Suspected stroke is an emergency. Rapid assessment determines treatment, followed by prevention of another event and rehabilitation.

condition:high-cholesterol.name: High cholesterol
condition:high-cholesterol.definition: Abnormal blood lipid levels can increase atherosclerotic cardiovascular risk.
summary: Abnormal blood lipid levels can increase atherosclerotic cardiovascular risk. Many people have no symptoms and learn about them through blood testing.
Bile-acid recycling and microbial transformations connect intestinal metabolism with lipid handling. Dietary fibre also acts through processes that include bile-acid binding and fermentation.
Care uses lipid measurements and overall cardiovascular risk to guide food changes and medicines. Inherited lipid disorders may need especially intensive treatment.

condition:gout.name: Gout
condition:gout.definition: Gout is inflammatory arthritis caused by urate crystals, often producing sudden severe pain in a joint.
summary: Gout is inflammatory arthritis caused by urate crystals, often producing sudden severe pain in a joint. Kidney handling of urate, genetics and metabolic factors contribute.
Intestinal urate transport and microbial purine metabolism are studied as additional parts of urate balance. These routes complement the established kidney and joint biology.
Acute attacks and long-term urate control require different treatment strategies. A clinician can guide anti-inflammatory treatment, urate-lowering therapy and relevant dietary changes.

condition:rheumatoid-arthritis.name: Rheumatoid arthritis
condition:rheumatoid-arthritis.definition: Rheumatoid arthritis is an autoimmune disease causing persistent joint inflammation, stiffness and potential damage.
summary: Rheumatoid arthritis is an autoimmune disease causing persistent joint inflammation, stiffness and potential damage. It can affect organs beyond the joints.
Studies investigate mucosal immune responses and microbes in the mouth and intestine before and after disease onset. The questions include microbial antigens, barrier function and treatment effects.
Early assessment and disease-modifying treatment help prevent damage. Care also includes activity, symptom control and monitoring for systemic effects.

condition:osteoarthritis.name: Osteoarthritis
condition:osteoarthritis.definition: Osteoarthritis involves changes across the whole joint, including cartilage, bone and surrounding tissues.
summary: Osteoarthritis involves changes across the whole joint, including cartilage, bone and surrounding tissues. Pain and reduced function often affect knees, hips or hands.
Researchers investigate metabolic inflammation and microbial products in joint symptoms. Mechanical loading, injury and local tissue changes remain essential parts of the condition.
Exercise, strength, weight management when relevant and pain treatment support function. Joint replacement is an option for some advanced disease.

condition:psoriasis.name: Psoriasis
condition:psoriasis.definition: Psoriasis is an immune-mediated condition producing inflamed, scaly skin.
summary: Psoriasis is an immune-mediated condition producing inflamed, scaly skin. Some people also develop psoriatic arthritis.

Research examines immune pathways shared between skin and gut, including microbial metabolites and inflammatory signalling. Skin communities and gut communities are separate habitats in these studies.
Treatment ranges from topical therapies to phototherapy and systemic medicines. Joint pain or swelling warrants assessment for associated arthritis.

condition:eczema.name: Atopic eczema
condition:eczema.definition: Atopic eczema causes itchy, inflamed skin with an impaired barrier.
summary: Atopic eczema causes itchy, inflamed skin with an impaired barrier. It often begins in childhood and can fluctuate with exposures and infection.
Early-life immune development and intestinal communities are studied alongside the skin barrier. Staphylococcus aureus on affected skin is a different, local microbial interaction.
Emollients, anti-inflammatory skin treatment and avoiding identified irritants support control. More severe disease can need specialist therapies.

condition:acne.name: Acne
condition:acne.definition: Acne develops in hair follicles through interactions among sebum, blocked pores, inflammation and Cutibacterium acnes.
summary: Acne develops in hair follicles through interactions among sebum, blocked pores, inflammation and Cutibacterium acnes. It can cause persistent scars and psychological distress.
Its direct microbial habitat is the skin follicle. Gut research explores dietary and systemic inflammatory connections, which are distinct from the established local skin mechanism.
Topical retinoids, benzoyl peroxide and other treatments are selected by severity. Persistent or scarring acne benefits from clinical assessment.

condition:rosacea.name: Rosacea
condition:rosacea.definition: Rosacea causes facial flushing, persistent redness and sometimes inflammatory bumps or eye symptoms.
summary: Rosacea causes facial flushing, persistent redness and sometimes inflammatory bumps or eye symptoms. Individual triggers and disease patterns vary.

Researchers investigate skin immunity, Demodex-associated responses and links with gastrointestinal conditions. These are several different biological routes rather than a single organism explaining all rosacea.
Sun protection, trigger management and prescribed skin or eye treatments support control. Eye pain or vision changes require assessment.

condition:seborrhoeic-dermatitis.name: Seborrhoeic dermatitis
condition:seborrhoeic-dermatitis.definition: Seborrhoeic dermatitis causes scaling and inflammation in oily skin areas such as the scalp, face and chest.
summary: Seborrhoeic dermatitis causes scaling and inflammation in oily skin areas such as the scalp, face and chest. Dandruff is a milder presentation.
Malassezia yeasts interact with skin lipids and host inflammatory responses. This is a local fungal habitat, which should be distinguished from Malassezia findings in gut research.
Antifungal shampoos or creams and short courses of anti-inflammatory treatments can help. Persistent or unusual presentations deserve assessment.

condition:asthma.name: Asthma
condition:asthma.definition: Asthma involves variable airway narrowing and inflammation, producing wheeze, breathlessness or cough.
summary: Asthma involves variable airway narrowing and inflammation, producing wheeze, breathlessness or cough. Triggers and inflammatory patterns differ between people.
Early-life gut communities and microbial metabolites are studied in the development of airway immunity. Respiratory and intestinal habitats are connected through host immune pathways.
Diagnosis uses the symptom pattern and breathing tests where appropriate. Inhaled treatment, trigger management and an action plan reduce attacks.

condition:allergic-rhinitis.name: Allergic rhinitis
condition:allergic-rhinitis.definition: Allergic rhinitis causes sneezing, itching, congestion and watery discharge after exposure to allergens such as pollen or dust mites..
summary: Allergic rhinitis causes sneezing, itching, congestion and watery discharge after exposure to allergens such as pollen or dust mites.
Studies investigate how microbial exposure and immune development influence allergic responses. The nasal community and intestinal community are different parts of that environment.
Allergen management, nasal corticosteroids, antihistamines and sometimes immunotherapy help control symptoms. Persistent obstruction can have additional causes.

condition:food-allergy.name: Food allergy
condition:food-allergy.definition: Food allergy is an immune reaction to a food and can affect the skin, gut, breathing or circulation.
summary: Food allergy is an immune reaction to a food and can affect the skin, gut, breathing or circulation. It differs from difficulty digesting a food such as lactose intolerance.
The intestinal barrier and development of immune tolerance are central research areas. Microbial metabolites are investigated for their effects on these processes.
Diagnosis uses history and appropriate testing, sometimes with supervised food challenges. Avoidance plans and emergency treatment are tailored to the confirmed allergy.

condition:anaphylaxis.name: Anaphylaxis
condition:anaphylaxis.definition: Anaphylaxis is a rapidly developing, potentially life-threatening allergic reaction involving breathing, circulation or several body systems..
summary: Anaphylaxis is a rapidly developing, potentially life-threatening allergic reaction involving breathing, circulation or several body systems.
Food can trigger anaphylaxis through immune pathways involving the gut, but the immediate event is a systemic emergency. Microbiome research on allergy prevention addresses a different timescale.
Use prescribed adrenaline promptly and call emergency services for suspected anaphylaxis. Follow-up identifies the trigger and establishes an emergency plan.

condition:chronic-urticaria.name: Chronic urticaria
condition:chronic-urticaria.definition: Chronic urticaria causes recurrent itchy wheals, sometimes with deeper swelling, for more than six weeks.
summary: Chronic urticaria causes recurrent itchy wheals, sometimes with deeper swelling, for more than six weeks. Many cases involve spontaneous immune activation rather than a specific food allergy.
Studies examine immune signalling, infections and intestinal communities in some patient groups. The clinical pattern and response to treatment are more informative than broad food-exclusion lists.
Antihistamines are commonly used, with specialist treatments for persistent disease. Breathing or circulatory symptoms with swelling need urgent care.

condition:lupus.name: Systemic lupus erythematosus
condition:lupus.definition: Lupus is an autoimmune disease that can affect skin, joints, kidneys, blood and other organs.
summary: Lupus is an autoimmune disease that can affect skin, joints, kidneys, blood and other organs. Its manifestations and activity vary substantially.
Research investigates microbial antigens and immune cross-reactivity at mucosal surfaces. These studies examine mechanisms that may differ between lupus subgroups.
Care follows the organs affected and can include antimalarial and immune-modifying medicines. Monitoring detects flares and treatment complications.

condition:multiple-sclerosis.name: Multiple sclerosis
condition:multiple-sclerosis.definition: Multiple sclerosis is an immune-mediated disease affecting the brain and spinal cord, producing varied neurological symptoms..
summary: Multiple sclerosis is an immune-mediated disease affecting the brain and spinal cord, producing varied neurological symptoms.
Human cohorts and experimental systems investigate intestinal microbes, metabolites and immune-cell activity. Disease-modifying medicines and disability can also alter the gut environment.
Neurological assessment and imaging guide diagnosis. Disease-modifying treatment, rehabilitation and symptom management address different parts of care.

condition:depression.name: Depression
condition:depression.definition: Depression affects mood, interest, thinking, sleep and daily function.
summary: Depression affects mood, interest, thinking, sleep and daily function. Physical symptoms and changes in appetite can accompany it.
Studies investigate gut microbial functions, immune signals and tryptophan metabolism in relation to mood. Human cohort findings and intervention studies answer different questions.
Psychological therapies, medicines and practical support are effective components of care. Severe impairment or thoughts of self-harm require prompt professional support.

condition:anxiety.name: Generalised anxiety disorder
condition:anxiety.definition: Generalised anxiety disorder involves persistent, difficult-to-control worry with physical tension, sleep disturbance or other symptoms affecting daily life..
summary: Generalised anxiety disorder involves persistent, difficult-to-control worry with physical tension, sleep disturbance or other symptoms affecting daily life.
The gut–brain relationship includes autonomic activity, immune signals and microbial metabolism. Stress can also change digestion, so direction of effect is part of the research.
Psychological therapy, appropriate medicines and support for sleep and daily function can help. Assessment also considers physical conditions or medicines that mimic anxiety.

condition:bipolar.name: Bipolar disorder
condition:bipolar.definition: Bipolar disorder involves episodes of depression and mania or hypomania, with changes in mood, energy, sleep and behaviour..
summary: Bipolar disorder involves episodes of depression and mania or hypomania, with changes in mood, energy, sleep and behaviour.
Microbial metabolism and inflammation are studied alongside established brain and circadian biology. Medicines, food intake and sleep changes are important influences on gut measurements.
Specialist assessment and mood-stabilising treatment are central. Recognising changes in sleep and early episode signs supports an individual care plan.

condition:schizophrenia.name: Schizophrenia
condition:schizophrenia.definition: Schizophrenia can involve hallucinations, delusions, disorganised thinking and changes in motivation or cognition.
summary: Schizophrenia can involve hallucinations, delusions, disorganised thinking and changes in motivation or cognition. It requires sustained clinical and social support.

Research examines immune signals, microbial metabolites and the effects of antipsychotic medicines on metabolic and intestinal health. These are complementary biological questions, not a replacement for psychiatric care.
Treatment combines appropriate medicines, psychological and social support and attention to physical health. New psychotic symptoms need prompt assessment.

condition:parkinsons.name: Parkinson’s disease
condition:parkinsons.definition: Parkinson’s disease affects movement and can also cause constipation, sleep changes and other non-motor symptoms..
summary: Parkinson’s disease affects movement and can also cause constipation, sleep changes and other non-motor symptoms.

The enteric nervous system, intestinal inflammation and microbial metabolism are studied in disease biology. Microbes can also metabolise some medicines, making treatment exposure an additional research question.
Neurological treatment, movement, rehabilitation and management of non-motor symptoms support function. Constipation and nutrition deserve attention alongside motor care.

condition:alzheimers.name: Alzheimer’s disease
condition:alzheimers.definition: Alzheimer’s disease causes progressive difficulties with memory and other cognitive functions.
summary: Alzheimer’s disease causes progressive difficulties with memory and other cognitive functions. Daily activities and independence become increasingly affected.
Studies examine microbial products, vascular health and immune signalling along the gut–brain axis. Food intake, ageing and medicines are also relevant to the gut environment in affected people.
Assessment distinguishes causes of cognitive decline. Care combines appropriate treatments, support for daily life and safety, and help for caregivers.

condition:migraine.name: Migraine
condition:migraine.definition: Migraine causes recurrent attacks of head pain with symptoms such as nausea, light sensitivity or aura.
summary: Migraine causes recurrent attacks of head pain with symptoms such as nausea, light sensitivity or aura. It is a neurological disorder with varied triggers.
Gut motility, nausea, shared signalling molecules and intestinal disorders are examined in migraine research. The connection also affects how oral medicines are absorbed during attacks.
Acute and preventive treatments are selected according to attack frequency and disability. A new or abrupt severe headache needs assessment for other causes.

condition:epilepsy.name: Epilepsy
condition:epilepsy.definition: Epilepsy involves a persistent tendency to recurrent seizures.
summary: Epilepsy involves a persistent tendency to recurrent seizures. Seizure types and underlying causes vary.
Dietary therapies for some drug-resistant epilepsies change metabolism and microbial substrates. Experimental work investigates which microbial functions participate in these treatment effects.
Diagnosis and antiseizure treatment are tailored to seizure type and cause. Specialised dietary treatment requires supervised nutritional and neurological care.

condition:autism.name: Autism spectrum condition
condition:autism.definition: Autism is a neurodevelopmental condition affecting communication, sensory processing and patterns of behaviour or interests.
summary: Autism is a neurodevelopmental condition affecting communication, sensory processing and patterns of behaviour or interests. Support needs vary widely.
Gut research often concerns co-occurring constipation, pain or feeding difficulties. Food selectivity, medicines and gastrointestinal symptoms are important when interpreting community measurements.
Support is individualised and includes communication, sensory and educational needs. Gastrointestinal symptoms deserve direct assessment.

condition:adhd.name: Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder
condition:adhd.definition: ADHD affects attention, impulse regulation or activity levels in ways that impair daily function.
summary: ADHD affects attention, impulse regulation or activity levels in ways that impair daily function. It can continue into adulthood.
Researchers study diet, microbial metabolites and gut–brain signalling alongside neurodevelopmental and genetic factors. Sleep and appetite changes can also affect the gut indirectly.
Assessment considers settings, functional difficulties and other conditions. Behavioural support, environmental adjustments and medicines can be helpful.

condition:insomnia.name: Insomnia
condition:insomnia.definition: Insomnia involves persistent difficulty falling asleep, staying asleep or waking too early with daytime consequences..
summary: Insomnia involves persistent difficulty falling asleep, staying asleep or waking too early with daytime consequences.

Sleep–wake timing and meals affect the intestinal environment. Human sleep-restriction studies measure changes in microbial richness and circulating metabolites rather than diagnosing insomnia from stool.
Cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia addresses persistent problems. Assessment also considers medicines, sleep apnoea and other contributing conditions.

condition:sleep-apnoea.name: Obstructive sleep apnoea
condition:sleep-apnoea.definition: Obstructive sleep apnoea causes repeated upper-airway collapse during sleep, with disrupted breathing and sleep quality..
summary: Obstructive sleep apnoea causes repeated upper-airway collapse during sleep, with disrupted breathing and sleep quality.
Intermittent low oxygen and metabolic changes are studied in relation to gut inflammation and microbial products. Obesity, diet and treatment are important accompanying factors.
Sleep testing establishes the diagnosis. Airway treatments, positive-pressure therapy and other interventions are chosen according to severity and anatomy.

condition:iron-deficiency.name: Iron-deficiency anaemia
condition:iron-deficiency.definition: Iron deficiency reduces the body’s capacity to make haemoglobin, causing fatigue, reduced exercise tolerance or other symptoms.
summary: Iron deficiency reduces the body’s capacity to make haemoglobin, causing fatigue, reduced exercise tolerance or other symptoms. Blood loss and inadequate absorption or intake are common routes.
The gut absorbs iron and is a site where blood loss or disease can create deficiency. Iron supplements also change the resources available to intestinal microbes.
Care identifies the cause as well as replacing iron. Heavy menstrual bleeding, gastrointestinal bleeding and coeliac disease are among the possible contributors.

condition:b12-deficiency.name: Vitamin B12 deficiency
condition:b12-deficiency.definition: B12 deficiency can cause anaemia, numbness, balance problems or cognitive symptoms.
summary: B12 deficiency can cause anaemia, numbness, balance problems or cognitive symptoms. Neurological effects can occur without obvious anaemia.
Absorption depends on stomach and small-intestinal processes, including intrinsic factor. Gastric autoimmunity, surgery, ileal disease and some medicines can interfere with this pathway.
Testing and the clinical picture guide oral or injected replacement. New neurological symptoms need timely assessment and treatment.

condition:hypothyroidism.name: Hypothyroidism
condition:hypothyroidism.definition: Hypothyroidism is insufficient thyroid hormone production, which can cause fatigue, cold intolerance, constipation and other changes..
summary: Hypothyroidism is insufficient thyroid hormone production, which can cause fatigue, cold intolerance, constipation and other changes.
Thyroid hormones influence intestinal motility. Research also examines autoimmune and microbial relationships, while constipation itself changes transit and fermentation.
Blood tests establish thyroid function. Hormone replacement and monitoring guide treatment; timing with food, iron and other medicines can affect absorption.

condition:hyperthyroidism.name: Hyperthyroidism
condition:hyperthyroidism.definition: Excess thyroid hormone can cause palpitations, heat intolerance, weight loss and frequent bowel movements.
summary: Excess thyroid hormone can cause palpitations, heat intolerance, weight loss and frequent bowel movements. Graves’ disease is a common cause.
Hormone-driven changes in transit and metabolism alter the digestive environment. Microbial findings need to be interpreted alongside these strong physiological effects.
Blood tests and investigation of the cause guide antithyroid medicines, radioiodine or surgery. Significant heart or systemic symptoms need prompt assessment.

condition:pcos.name: Polycystic ovary syndrome
condition:pcos.definition: PCOS involves combinations of ovulatory dysfunction, androgen excess and characteristic ovarian findings.
summary: PCOS involves combinations of ovulatory dysfunction, androgen excess and characteristic ovarian findings. Insulin resistance and metabolic risks are common.

Studies examine microbial metabolites and metabolic inflammation alongside hormonal and reproductive features. Food patterns, body composition and medicines are important influences on the measurements.
Care follows the person’s priorities, including cycles, symptoms, fertility and metabolic health. Nutrition, activity and appropriate medicines are selected accordingly.

condition:endometriosis.name: Endometriosis
condition:endometriosis.definition: Endometriosis involves tissue similar to the uterine lining growing outside the uterus.
summary: Endometriosis involves tissue similar to the uterine lining growing outside the uterus. Pelvic pain, painful periods and fertility difficulties can result.
Intestinal symptoms can overlap with pelvic disease. Research investigates immune activity, hormone metabolism and microbial communities at several body sites.
Assessment and treatment can include pain management, hormonal therapy or surgery according to symptoms and fertility goals. Bowel symptoms also warrant their own evaluation.

condition:periodontitis.name: Periodontitis
condition:periodontitis.definition: Periodontitis is inflammatory destruction of tissues supporting the teeth.
summary: Periodontitis is inflammatory destruction of tissues supporting the teeth. It can lead to gum recession, loose teeth and tooth loss.
Dental biofilms and host inflammation directly drive the local disease process. Oral organisms and inflammatory signals are also studied in relation to systemic and gut conditions.
Professional periodontal treatment and sustained daily plaque control are central. Smoking, diabetes and other contributing factors affect disease and healing.

condition:dental-caries.name: Dental caries
condition:dental-caries.definition: Dental caries develops when repeated acid production in dental plaque causes mineral loss from teeth.
summary: Dental caries develops when repeated acid production in dental plaque causes mineral loss from teeth. Sugar exposure, saliva and fluoride influence the balance.
This is a clear community-and-chemistry mechanism: oral microbes ferment carbohydrates, lowering local pH. Frequent exposures can sustain conditions favouring acid-tolerant organisms.
Fluoride, effective cleaning, sugar-exposure patterns and dental treatment address different stages. Pain, swelling or a dental abscess need prompt care.

condition:gingivitis.name: Gingivitis
condition:gingivitis.definition: Gingivitis is inflammation of the gums, often causing bleeding with cleaning.
summary: Gingivitis is inflammation of the gums, often causing bleeding with cleaning. It can improve when dental plaque and contributing factors are addressed.
A biofilm accumulates at the gum margin and stimulates a local immune response. The same organisms can behave differently in a changed community and habitat.
Daily plaque control and professional cleaning support recovery. Persistent bleeding should be checked for periodontal disease and other contributors.

condition:common-cold.name: Common cold
condition:common-cold.definition: The common cold is a viral upper-respiratory infection causing a runny nose, sore throat and cough.
summary: The common cold is a viral upper-respiratory infection causing a runny nose, sore throat and cough. Several different viruses can produce the syndrome.
The primary infected habitat is respiratory. Gut research examines immune development and host responses to infections, rather than treating the cold as an intestinal infection.
Rest, fluids and symptom relief are usually sufficient. Antibiotics do not treat cold viruses; difficulty breathing or persistent worsening symptoms warrant assessment.

condition:influenza.name: Influenza
condition:influenza.definition: Influenza is a respiratory viral infection that can cause fever, muscle aches, cough and marked fatigue.
summary: Influenza is a respiratory viral infection that can cause fever, muscle aches, cough and marked fatigue. Some people develop serious complications.

Experimental work investigates how intestinal microbes and their products influence antiviral immunity. The virus primarily infects the respiratory tract, distinguishing the immune link from the infected site.
Vaccination reduces risk. Antiviral treatment is particularly important for severe illness or higher-risk people and is most useful when started promptly.

condition:covid.name: COVID-19
condition:covid.definition: COVID-19 can affect the respiratory tract and other systems and sometimes causes gastrointestinal symptoms.
summary: COVID-19 can affect the respiratory tract and other systems and sometimes causes gastrointestinal symptoms. Severity and recovery vary.
SARS-CoV-2 can involve intestinal cells. Research follows gut-community changes, immune activity and persistent symptoms, alongside effects of medicines and illness severity.
Testing, risk assessment and current treatment guidance inform care. Breathing difficulty or other severe symptoms need urgent assessment; persistent symptoms deserve follow-up.

condition:pneumonia.name: Pneumonia
condition:pneumonia.definition: Pneumonia is infection of lung tissue caused by bacteria, viruses or other organisms.
summary: Pneumonia is infection of lung tissue caused by bacteria, viruses or other organisms. It can cause cough, fever, breathlessness and chest pain.
The mouth and respiratory tract can provide organisms involved in infection. Research also examines gut-mediated immune responses and the intestinal effects of antibiotic treatment.
Assessment establishes severity and likely cause. Treatment can involve antibiotics, antivirals, oxygen or supportive care according to the infection and the person’s condition.

condition:sinusitis.name: Sinusitis
condition:sinusitis.definition: Sinusitis involves inflammation of the sinus lining, commonly following a viral infection or with ongoing inflammatory disease.
summary: Sinusitis involves inflammation of the sinus lining, commonly following a viral infection or with ongoing inflammatory disease. Facial pressure and nasal symptoms are common.
The local microbial habitat is the nose and sinuses. Treatments such as antibiotics can also affect intestinal communities; these are different sites and mechanisms.
Care depends on duration, severity and cause. Most short viral episodes do not need antibiotics, while persistent or complicated disease warrants assessment.

condition:breast-cancer.name: Breast cancer
condition:breast-cancer.definition: Breast cancer includes several tumour types with different hormone receptors and molecular features.
summary: Breast cancer includes several tumour types with different hormone receptors and molecular features. These distinctions guide treatment.
Research explores microbial hormone metabolism, immune signalling and interactions with cancer therapies. The gut route is a research context alongside established tumour biology and inherited risk.
Screening, imaging and biopsy establish the diagnosis. Surgery, radiotherapy and systemic treatments are selected according to stage and tumour characteristics.

mechanism:dietary-iron.name: Dietary iron
mechanism:dietary-iron.definition: Iron released from food reaches the absorptive surface of the small intestine.

mechanism:enterocyte.name: Enterocyte
mechanism:enterocyte.definition: An absorptive cell takes up iron and can retain it in ferritin.

mechanism:ferroportin.name: Ferroportin
mechanism:ferroportin.definition: The exporter releases iron from enterocytes and iron-recycling cells.

mechanism:transferrin-bound-iron.name: Transferrin-bound iron
mechanism:transferrin-bound-iron.definition: Transferrin carries iron to tissues, including bone marrow.

mechanism:marrow-and-recycling.name: Marrow and recycling
mechanism:marrow-and-recycling.definition: Marrow makes red cells; macrophages recover iron from ageing red cells.

mechanism:hepcidin.name: Hepcidin
mechanism:hepcidin.definition: This liver hormone reduces the number of active ferroportin exporters.

mechanism:released-serotonin.name: Released serotonin
mechanism:released-serotonin.definition: Serotonin activates nearby receptors involved in movement, fluid and electrolyte secretion, sensation and immune responses. Its effect depends on the receptor and tissue.

mechanism:enteric-and-sensory-nerves.name: Enteric and sensory nerves
mechanism:enteric-and-sensory-nerves.definition: Enteric circuits coordinate digestive reflexes. Serotonin can also activate receptors on sensory fibres, including vagal afferents that relay gut information toward the brainstem.

mechanism:platelet-uptake.name: Platelet uptake
mechanism:platelet-uptake.definition: Platelets take up peripheral serotonin through SERT and store it. On activation they release it into vascular, clotting and inflammatory responses. This circulating reservoir has a different destination from serotonin made inside the brain.

mechanism:microbial-metabolites.name: Microbial metabolites
mechanism:microbial-metabolites.definition: Products of microbial metabolism influence enterochromaffin-cell activity.

mechanism:liver-bile-acids.name: Liver bile acids
mechanism:liver-bile-acids.definition: The liver makes primary bile acids and secretes them into bile.

mechanism:digestive-bile-pool.name: Digestive bile pool
mechanism:digestive-bile-pool.definition: Bile acids participate in fat digestion and absorption.

mechanism:microbial-transformations.name: Microbial transformations
mechanism:microbial-transformations.definition: Deconjugation and further transformations alter the bile-acid mixture.

mechanism:ileal-uptake.name: Ileal uptake
mechanism:ileal-uptake.definition: Most bile acids return through the portal circulation.

mechanism:fxr-fgf19.name: FXR → FGF19
mechanism:fxr-fgf19.definition: An intestinal feedback signal regulates liver synthesis.

mechanism:immune-receptors.name: Immune receptors
mechanism:immune-receptors.definition: Specific bile-acid derivatives influence immune-cell differentiation.

mechanism:fermentable-fibre.name: Fermentable fibre
mechanism:fermentable-fibre.definition: Plant carbohydrates and resistant starch supply microbial substrates.

mechanism:primary-degraders.name: Primary degraders
mechanism:primary-degraders.definition: Organisms break down complex carbohydrates and release fermentation products.

mechanism:acetate-and-lactate.name: Acetate and lactate
mechanism:acetate-and-lactate.definition: Products made by one organism become substrates for another.

mechanism:colonocytes.name: Colonocytes
mechanism:colonocytes.definition: These cells consume butyrate as an energy source.

mechanism:portal-and-systemic-pools.name: Portal and systemic pools
mechanism:portal-and-systemic-pools.definition: Acetate, propionate and butyrate have different rates of uptake and use.

mechanism:microbial-indoles.name: Microbial indoles
mechanism:microbial-indoles.definition: Microbial enzymes create chemically diverse indole derivatives.

mechanism:ahr-receptor.name: AhR receptor
mechanism:ahr-receptor.definition: A chemical sensor activated by particular ligands.

mechanism:il-22-response.name: IL-22 response
mechanism:il-22-response.definition: A cytokine pathway involved in epithelial defence.

mechanism:kynurenine-pathway.name: Kynurenine pathway
mechanism:kynurenine-pathway.definition: Host IDO/TDO enzymes and microbial activities metabolise tryptophan along this branch.

mechanism:serotonin-pathway.name: Serotonin pathway
mechanism:serotonin-pathway.definition: A separate branch supplies peripheral or brain serotonin synthesis.

mechanism:food-b12.name: Food B12
mechanism:food-b12.definition: Digestion releases B12 from food proteins.

mechanism:intrinsic-factor-complex.name: Intrinsic-factor complex
mechanism:intrinsic-factor-complex.definition: B12 binds intrinsic factor after earlier digestive binding steps.

mechanism:cubam-uptake.name: Cubam uptake
mechanism:cubam-uptake.definition: Cubilin and amnionless enable uptake of the complex.

mechanism:host-b12-supply.name: Host B12 supply
mechanism:host-b12-supply.definition: Absorbed B12 supports human enzyme reactions.

mechanism:microbial-corrinoids.name: Microbial corrinoids
mechanism:microbial-corrinoids.definition: Some microbes synthesise B12 or related corrinoids.

mechanism:microbial-importers.name: Microbial importers
mechanism:microbial-importers.definition: Other organisms rely on uptake and compete for available cofactors.

mechanism:goblet-cells.name: Goblet cells
mechanism:goblet-cells.definition: Specialised epithelial cells secrete MUC2 mucin.

mechanism:inner-mucus.name: Inner mucus
mechanism:inner-mucus.definition: A dense protective layer in the healthy colon.

mechanism:outer-mucus.name: Outer mucus
mechanism:outer-mucus.definition: Expanded mucus creates a microbial habitat.

mechanism:mucin-foragers.name: Mucin foragers
mechanism:mucin-foragers.definition: Organisms release and consume mucus-derived sugars.

mechanism:epithelial-surface.name: Epithelial surface
mechanism:epithelial-surface.definition: The cell layer underlying the mucus boundary.

mechanism:bacterial-molecules.name: Bacterial molecules
mechanism:bacterial-molecules.definition: Structures such as B. fragilis polysaccharide A reach host sensors.

mechanism:tlr2-sensing.name: TLR2 sensing
mechanism:tlr2-sensing.definition: A receptor recognises particular microbial signals.

mechanism:regulatory-t-cells.name: Regulatory T cells
mechanism:regulatory-t-cells.definition: These cells help regulate immune responses.

mechanism:foxp3-regulation.name: Foxp3 regulation
mechanism:foxp3-regulation.definition: Gene regulation supports regulatory T-cell identity.

mechanism:community-combinations.name: Community combinations
mechanism:community-combinations.definition: Signals from several organisms can alter the combined cytokine response.

mechanism:fermenting-bacteria.name: Fermenting bacteria
mechanism:fermenting-bacteria.definition: Carbohydrate fermentation releases hydrogen and other products.

mechanism:hydrogen-and-formate.name: Hydrogen and formate
mechanism:hydrogen-and-formate.definition: Electron-rich products pass between microbial partners.

mechanism:methanogenic-archaea.name: Methanogenic archaea
mechanism:methanogenic-archaea.definition: Methanogens use suitable substrates to make methane.

mechanism:methane.name: Methane
mechanism:methane.definition: Gas can leave in breath or intestinal gas.

mechanism:other-hydrogen-consumers.name: Other hydrogen consumers
mechanism:other-hydrogen-consumers.definition: Acetogens and sulfate reducers provide competing routes.

mechanism:acetate-or-sulfide.name: Acetate or sulfide
mechanism:acetate-or-sulfide.definition: Different consumers produce different end products.

mechanism:luminal-chemicals.name: Luminal chemicals
mechanism:luminal-chemicals.definition: Nutrients and microbial metabolites stimulate host sensory cells.

mechanism:enteric-neural-circuits.name: Enteric neural circuits
mechanism:enteric-neural-circuits.definition: Neural networks coordinate motor and secretory responses.

mechanism:smooth-muscle-and-transit.name: Smooth muscle and transit
mechanism:smooth-muscle-and-transit.definition: Contraction patterns move and mix intestinal contents.

mechanism:muscularis-macrophages.name: Muscularis macrophages
mechanism:muscularis-macrophages.definition: Immune cells signal to enteric neurons through BMP2.

mechanism:neuronal-csf1.name: Neuronal CSF1
mechanism:neuronal-csf1.definition: Neurons provide a survival signal to local macrophages.

mechanism:gut-activity.name: Gut activity
mechanism:gut-activity.definition: Food, microbes, movement and host sensory cells generate several kinds of signals at once.

mechanism:sensory-nerve-fibres.name: Sensory nerve fibres
mechanism:sensory-nerve-fibres.definition: Vagal and other sensory pathways carry information toward the central nervous system. Local serotonin can activate nerve receptors; neuropod cells can also signal through glutamate.

mechanism:brain-networks.name: Brain networks
mechanism:brain-networks.definition: Incoming visceral information meets brain circuits involved in appetite, sensation, stress and behaviour. Brain serotonin is made locally from imported tryptophan.

mechanism:tryptophan-availability.name: Tryptophan availability
mechanism:tryptophan-availability.definition: Tryptophan can cross the blood–brain barrier. Host and microbial metabolism influence its availability and its conversion into serotonin, kynurenine and indole-related products.

mechanism:immune-and-metabolic-signals.name: Immune and metabolic signals
mechanism:immune-and-metabolic-signals.definition: Barrier biology, immune mediators and microbial metabolites connect gut activity with host responses. Their effects involve several intermediary cells and tissues.

mechanism:autonomic-and-stress-output.name: Autonomic and stress output
mechanism:autonomic-and-stress-output.definition: Autonomic nerves and the hypothalamic–pituitary–adrenal system change digestive conditions, including motor, secretory and immune activity.

process:living-well:fibre.name: Feed a community
process:living-well:fibre.definition: Different fibres open different microbial pathways.

process:living-well:fermented.name: Food already transformed
process:living-well:fermented.definition: Microbes change food before it reaches you.

process:living-well:movement.name: Move the ecosystem
process:living-well:movement.definition: Exercise changes the host that microbes live in.

process:living-well:sleep.name: A daily rhythm
process:living-well:sleep.definition: Sleep changes the conditions of microbial life.

process:living-well:mood.name: Signals and experience
process:living-well:mood.definition: Microbes participate in the body’s chemical conversation.

process:living-well:digestion.name: Make room for digestion
process:living-well:digestion.definition: Transit shapes the ecosystem as food moves through it.

process:living-well:resistant-starch.name: Resistant starch
process:living-well:resistant-starch.definition: Some starch feeds microbes after escaping our own digestion.

process:living-well:pulses.name: Beans, lentils & chickpeas
process:living-well:pulses.definition: A meal can deliver protein and microbial food together.

process:living-well:breakfast.name: Oats, fruit & live yoghurt
process:living-well:breakfast.definition: Combine a plant substrate with a food transformed by microbes.

process:living-well:oral-care.name: Care for the mouth’s ecosystem
process:living-well:oral-care.definition: Repeated sugar exposure reshapes a microbial habitat before food reaches the stomach.

process:living-well:fasting.name: Fasting
process:living-well:fasting.definition: Intermittent fasting, Ramadan, ketosis and the importance of timing, nutrition and life stage.
summary: Intermittent fasting, Ramadan, ketosis and the importance of timing, nutrition and life stage.

process:living-well:daily-eating-windows.name: Daily eating windows
process:living-well:daily-eating-windows.definition: Early, late and self-selected schedules put timing to a direct test.

process:living-well:longer-fasts.name: Longer fasts & refeeding
process:living-well:longer-fasts.definition: Clinical fasting studies follow what happens during the fast and after food returns.

process:fermentation:yoghurt.name: Yoghurt
process:fermentation:yoghurt.definition: A partnership that turns milk into a soft gel.

process:fermentation:sauerkraut.name: Sauerkraut
process:fermentation:sauerkraut.definition: A succession of bacteria under the brine.

process:fermentation:tempeh.name: Tempeh
process:fermentation:tempeh.definition: A fungus weaves beans into a food.

process:fermentation:kefir.name: Kefir
process:fermentation:kefir.definition: A grain carries a community of bacteria and yeasts.

process:fermentation:kimchi.name: Kimchi
process:fermentation:kimchi.definition: Vegetables become a changing acidic habitat.

process:fermentation:sourdough.name: Sourdough
process:fermentation:sourdough.definition: Bacteria and yeasts raise a dough together.

process:fermentation:miso.name: Miso
process:fermentation:miso.definition: Koji enzymes and a salt-tolerant community transform a paste.

process:fermentation:kombucha.name: Kombucha
process:fermentation:kombucha.definition: Tea transformed by a partnership of yeasts and acetic-acid bacteria.

process:fermentation:water-kefir.name: Water kefir
process:fermentation:water-kefir.definition: A dairy-free fermentation held together by living grains.

process:fermentation:dill-pickles.name: Fermented dill pickles
process:fermentation:dill-pickles.definition: Cucumbers become sour through microbial fermentation.

process:fermentation:fermented-carrots.name: Fermented carrots
process:fermentation:fermented-carrots.definition: A simple vegetable ferment with a sweet starting material.

process:illness-recovery:helicobacter.name: H. pylori
process:illness-recovery:helicobacter.definition: A bacterium makes a home in stomach mucus.

process:illness-recovery:cdiff.name: C. difficile
process:illness-recovery:cdiff.definition: A disturbed community loses some of its protection.

process:illness-recovery:norovirus.name: Norovirus
process:illness-recovery:norovirus.definition: A human-cell virus in the intestinal ecosystem.

process:illness-recovery:giardia.name: Giardia
process:illness-recovery:giardia.definition: A protist attaches to the small-intestinal surface.

process:illness-recovery:ongoing-symptom.name: Ongoing gut symptoms
process:illness-recovery:ongoing-symptom.definition: Follow mechanisms without forcing one microbial explanation.

fermented-food-diet.name: A varied fermented-food diet
fermented-food-diet.definition: A dietary pattern containing several fermented foods.

varied-fibre-foods.name: Varied sources of dietary fibre
varied-fibre-foods.definition: A dietary pattern drawing fibre from several food groups.

toilet-posture.name: Toilet posture
toilet-posture.definition: Hip flexion, foot support and comfortable positioning can change the mechanics of bowel emptying.
summary: Hip flexion, foot support and comfortable positioning can change the mechanics of bowel emptying.

anal-skin.name: Skin around the anus
anal-skin.definition: External perianal skin is the area cleaned after passing stool; it is distinct from the rectum inside the body.
summary: External perianal skin is the area cleaned after passing stool; it is distinct from the rectum inside the body.

anal-cleansing.name: Anal cleansing
anal-cleansing.definition: Gentle external removal of stool using paper, water or both; internal irrigation is a different intervention.
summary: Gentle external removal of stool using paper, water or both; internal irrigation is a different intervention.

cooking-method.name: Cooking method
cooking-method.definition: Heat, water, time and food structure jointly affect texture, safety and digestion.
summary: Heat, water, time and food structure jointly affect texture, safety and digestion.

eating-pace.name: Eating pace
eating-pace.definition: The rate at which a meal is consumed can influence intake during that meal.
summary: The rate at which a meal is consumed can influence intake during that meal.

ketone-bodies.name: Ketone bodies
ketone-bodies.definition: Liver-derived fuels produced from fat; their concentration depends on feeding, activity and metabolic state.
summary: Liver-derived fuels produced from fat; their concentration depends on feeding, activity and metabolic state.

energy-availability.name: Energy availability
energy-availability.definition: Energy remaining for physiological functions after exercise expenditure; it can differ even at the same fasting duration.
summary: Energy remaining for physiological functions after exercise expenditure; it can differ even at the same fasting duration.

process:living-well:toilet-posture-care.name: Passing stool & cleaning afterwards
process:living-well:toilet-posture-care.definition: Posture, gentle anal care and the cultural life of the toilet.
summary: Posture, gentle anal care and the cultural life of the toilet.

process:living-well:slow-cooking-eating.name: Slow cooking & slow eating
process:living-well:slow-cooking-eating.definition: What time changes in the pot, in the mouth and during a meal.
summary: What time changes in the pot, in the mouth and during a meal.

mechanism:mitochondria-0.name: Fibre and butyrate
mechanism:mitochondria-0.definition: Fibre-fermenting communities supply butyrate, a major oxidative fuel for the colon lining.

mechanism:mitochondria-1.name: Colon-cell mitochondria
mechanism:mitochondria-1.definition: Butyrate is converted to acetyl-CoA. The citric acid cycle and electron transport chain use this fuel and oxygen to support ATP production.

mechanism:mitochondria-2.name: Low-oxygen habitat
mechanism:mitochondria-2.definition: Oxygen consumption by the lining helps preserve the low-oxygen environment occupied by many gut fermenters.

mechanism:mitochondria-3.name: Microbial hydrogen sulfide
mechanism:mitochondria-3.definition: Microbial sulfur metabolism supplies hydrogen sulfide at the epithelial surface.

mechanism:mitochondria-4.name: Sulfide oxidation
mechanism:mitochondria-4.definition: SQOR transfers electrons from sulfide to the coenzyme Q pool. Further oxidation disposes of sulfide; excess sulfide inhibits complex IV.

mechanism:mitochondria-5.name: Food polyphenols
mechanism:mitochondria-5.definition: Ellagitannins and ellagic acid in foods such as pomegranates, berries and walnuts provide substrates for urolithin-producing communities.

mechanism:mitochondria-6.name: Urolithin-producing community
mechanism:mitochondria-6.definition: Gordonibacter species produce intermediates; additional community reactions complete conversion to urolithin A.

mechanism:mitochondria-7.name: Urolithin A
mechanism:mitochondria-7.definition: A microbial metabolite links food transformation to experiments on mitochondrial quality control in distant tissues.

mechanism:mitochondria-8.name: Mitophagy and muscle
mechanism:mitochondria-8.definition: Cells recycle damaged mitochondria through mitophagy. Animal experiments and human trials examine consequences for respiration and muscle performance.
